War reawakens mans primitive

phenomenon which gem experts

Whereas the diamond, emerald

stones which have not been sought

Chief among these stones is the

popular with smart women.


Ancient records concerning the

ment. Their legions were stationed

The sedition trial, which during
its seven months has brought nearly
every legal situation possible to a
courtroom, achieved something new
yesterday mute session.


After these months of wordy
hours, the transcript disclosed today
that not syllable of spoken testi-
mony was given yesterday and that
the heavy, unprecedented silence
was broken by only few words from
the bench, announcing the neces-
sary formalities of recesses and ad-
journment and stray tilt between
counsel toward the close.


Now" remarked a weary attorney
as the curious day ended, I've seen
everything"


Examine Exhibits.
The session was devoted to the
examination of Government exhibits
by the jury. These included lengthy
bulletins of the American National
ist Confederation. self-styled Fas-
cist party which was headed by
George E. Deatherage, q defendant
and other documents. Correspond
ence attributed to other defendants
was among the papers which the
jurors read.


1t looked as if the day would pass
without word spoken by counsel
on either side But just before ad-
tournament, Ethelbert B. Frey, at
torney for Robert E. Edmondson
suggested that the record show with
which exhibits the jury had beer
occupied for five hours.
Prosecutor Rogge said the record
Of the previous day already dis
closed that.


Il don't know what Mr.. Rogge has
produced" Mr.. Frey objected. eve
should know"


Implication Expunged.


Il don't conduct cases that way
Mr.. Rogge retorted. Maybe you do >


Chief Justice Edward c. Eicher
expunged Mr.. Frey's implication
from the record and court was ad-
journed for the day.


The session was marked by the
return of Mrs. Lois de Lafayette
'Washburn, a defendant, who had
been absent, with the courts per-
mission, for something like three
months. Mrs. Washburn has had a
job which prevented her from at
tending the trial. Frank w. Clark
another defendant who has been
away for month for a similar rea-
son, also was back for the day. The
two took their old seats beside their
attorney, Ira Chase Koehne.


Apples for Defendants.


Mrs. Washburn had bag of
apples for Hans Diebel, another of
the rs alleged conspirators on trial
Diebel passed around the apples to
other defendants.


The last Government witness,
Henry D. Allen, completed his testi-
mony Monday night. Mr.. Rogge did
not announce who the next witness
would be, but he was expected to
identify today some new exhibits.

bors became alarmed at the noise

Marshal Kesselring, whose blunder
permitted the almost unopposed Allied
landing a short distance below Rome a
little more than week ago, struck
viciously with everything he had avail
able in an effort to smash the units of
the 5th Army operating in front of the
Gustave line in the hope that he could

LONDON, Aug. Turkey
broke off diplomatic and eco
nomic relations with Germany
today in an action which Berlin
broadcasts declared must be re-
garded as a prelude to war"


This setback for Hitler on the
Balkan flank followed a govern
mental shift in Helsinki which was
believed the first step toward tax
ing Finland out of the war as a CO.
belligerent of the Reich. This shift
moved Marshal Baron Carl Gustaf
Mannerheim to the presidency to
succeed Risto Ryti. who resigned.
Turkeys severance of ties with
Germany was disclosed by the
Turkish home radio and was con-
/ f1rmed almost Immediately by Ber-
lin brosdcasts.


Premier Sukru Saracoglu an
nounced the cabinets decision to
make the break, telling the National
Assembly that it had been requested
by Britain, with American support.
The Assembly promptly ratified the
decision.


Aid Promised by Britain.
Britain had promised Turkey
economic and financial help and
war equipment" the Premier said,
Ito meet the difficulties which would
arise" from the action.
The break is effective at midnight
tonight.


Speaking before Alb delegates of
the assembly. Saracoglu said the step
did not mean that Turkey would
enter the war, but that such a pos
sibility would depend on the atti-
tude of the other side"


This indicated that Turkey. which
has more than 1000 900 well-trained
soldiers, would enter the fight only
if Germany started hostile action.


Saracoglu said that Britain, with
American support, had asked Tur-
key within the limits of our agree
ment mutual assistance alliance)
to break diplomatic and economic
relations" with Germany.


The break-a major blow to Ger
man prestige-may have an inn
portant effect on shaky Balkan
satellites, particularly Bulgaria,
which has shown increasing indica-
tions recently of desiring to leave
the company of Germany and move
closer to Russia.


Trade Already Drastically Cut.
Turkish trade with Germany al
ready is drastically reduced. Tur-
key cut off shipments of chrome
several months ago. Such strategic
materials as cotton. copper, fish,
oil-seeds and mohair now will be
barred.


The Axis had wind of the trend
before the action was taken. Berlin
broadcasters had warned the Turks
that break in diplomatic and eco
nomic relations would mean war.
Rumors circulated in Ankara that
the japanese were about to break
of diplomatic relations with Tur-
key.


Advices from Turkey made no
mention of granting air or sea bases
to the Allies.


The most immediate and direct
effect of the break, aside from the
cutting off of German supply lines
from Turkey, apparently will be the
closing of the German Embassy and
consulates which have given the
Nazis valuable observation posts in
the Middle East.


Presumably hundreds of agents
and private German nationals also
will be expelled or placed under
close watch, Gripping Berlins es-
pionage still further.

WnaJ started out last summer as
q daylight reconnaissance mission
against the Japanese supply base of
Kavieng on New Ireland Island de-
veloped into game of hide-and-
seek with eight Zeros and ended in
perilous parachute leap for IL of
our airmen who trekked three days
through dense jungles to return to
their base in New Guinea.


Staff Sergt. Carl Polvinale, 25,
Of 2420 L'Enfant square Sc,
who recently returned home, was
the nose gunner on that bomb
er. 10 him, the wearer of the Dis
tinguished Flying Cross with Oak
Leaf Cluster, the episode was just
another of SO hazardous missions
against the Japanese. But what he
had been through was mirrored on
the faces of his wife and mother,
Mrs. Lucy Polvinale, who listened
attentively in the living room of
their home.


The mission began in the early
morning. Except for the usual
tenseness among the crew and
rough weather all went well at first.
The bomber maneuvered over Ka-
vieng for special photographer to
make his shots.


Eight Zeros Attack.


Suddenly, just as the bomber
headed towards home, eight zeros
sWarmed in and attacked from all
sides. Bursts of 25-millimeter shells
caused the No. engine to catch
fire. One of the waist guns was
out, the other had to be hand
charged. The top turret gun
wouldn't fire regularly, one of Sergt.
Polvinale's nose guns broke down,
leaving him unprotected from the
right side.


From then on it was nip and tuck,
with the bomber ducking into rain
SQUALLS and clouds and the Zeros
swarming around for the kill. Three
of the Zeros disappeared and were
later tailed as probables. But the
others continued to riddle the
bomber. BY using special carbon
dioxide extinguisher the pilot was
able to put out the blaze on the
now-useless No. l engine. The gun
ners were forced to hand-charge
their guns and many times had 70
stand back helplessly as the Japs
zoomed by.


Coming out of one thick rain
squall, the bomber's crew found
themselves directly over four Jap
destroyers. and for the first time
realized why they were meeting with
so much opposition. The destroyers
filled the sky with ack-ack shells
and only by a quick turn was the
bomber able to get out of range.
The enemy fighters, however, kept
coming. When the fighters ap-
peared almost out of shells they
swooped in threateningly without
firing, Finally, they gave up the
chase.


Engine Begins Sputtering.


BY this time new menace had
arisen-the bomber's No. engine
began sputtering. The plane would
gain altitude and then suddenly
drop, but the crew nursed her home
ward. Soon the New Guinea coast
appeared below, then the dense
jungles. Almost home, but not
quite, the No. 2 engine was working
irregularly. After a hurried confer
ence with the engineer, the pilot an
nounced through the interphones
they would all have to jump.


One by one the crew leaped out,
with the pilot and co-pilot gong
last. Sergt Polivinale recalls how
the opening of his chute seemed to
jerk his body apart 1t was his first
jump. He landed in tall, wiry grass
that bruised him painfully.

Liberator staggered home, with a
safe but shaken crew.

Thousands Of Yanks know Suva,

Tiny? Land area of Fiji almost

Cannibals? Fiji's notoriety was

South Pacific Ocean target with

NEW YORK, Jan. 6.-Donald M.
Nelson, chairman of the War Produc-
ton Board, has been asked to take
immediate action on reports that
Federal agencies here have been
burning waste paper in the City
Sanitation Departments incinerator.


The request was made yesterday
by Edwin S. Friendly, national chair
man of the Waste Paper Salvage
Campaign of the American News
paper Publishers Association, after
the New York Daily News said the
Office of War Information, the Office
of Price Administration and the
Federal Works Agency had burned
423, 500 pounds of paper in the past
six months.


1t also was reported that H. M.
Faust, WPB salvage director in
Washington, had ordered Clinton
White, WPB regional salvage head
here, to make an investigation.


j. B. Straley, regional director Of
the Office for Emergency Manage
ment, Federal holding company for
all emergency agencies, denied that
the OPA and owl had practiced
widespread burning of waste paper.


He reported that the OPA had
burned some spare ration coupons
and the Owl had informed him
secret and confidential matter had
been incinerated during the past
year. but that nothing has been
burned since the waste paper drive
began.


Regional FWA Director John M.
Gallagher said that when the Works
Progress Administration was liqui-
dated bids for $4,000 pounds of paper
were asked, but none received, so
the paper was burned.


He said FWA trucks had picked
up waste paper from Federal Offices
other than the FWA and had de-
livered it to the incinerator, but
that the FWA's own waste paper
was delivered to a contractor.

LONDON, Dec. 80. More than
1000 British-based American bomb
ers and fighting planes pierced
through fog today and pounded
German supply lines to the western
front for the eighth consecutive
day.


Eight bombers and three fighters
were reported missing from these
operations.


While the German air force stuck
close to its bases for third day,
more than 1900 Flying Fortresses
and Liberators of the 9th Air Force,
escorted by approximately 700
Thunderbolds and Mustangs, struck
unmolested at railroad bridges on
lines leading directly from Berlin
and at freight yards at Mannheim,
Kaiserlautern and Kassel.


The points attacked on the roads
from Berlin were not specified.


The. Americans encountered only
moderate fire from German anti
aircraft guns, headquarters of the
United States Strategic Air Forces
In Europe said.


A heavy toll of German supplies
already had been taken by Allied
air attacks. the 9Th Air Force re-
ported. 1t said reconnaissance
photographs of yesterdays raid on
Frankfurt's railyard showed at least
1900 freight cars, most of them
carrying ammunition and oil, were
destroyed and that a bridge, bar
racks, roundhouses, warehouses and
industrial targets had been dam
aged.


Bad weather apparently grounded
the 18th United States Air Force in
Italy today and dispatches from the
front lines on the western front
indicated that the weather was not
favorable to large-scale operations
by fighter bomber units based on
the continent.

Deliberately, and with malice

unhinged.


Handcuffed Giants.

former teammate, Arnie Herber,

quent in the pro game

locked at center and went all the
way to the %. Fritsch followed

1t seemed only a question of who

but the middle of the Giants line
went to work with a vengeance at

MOSCOW, April 22.-The Soviet,
who have won such brilliant VIC
tories on the military and diplo-
matte fronts, have turned on a home
front offensive with the opening of
unrationed food stores and a gen.
eral improvement program.


Foreign observers well versed in
Soviet policy-making attach consid-
erable Importance to the stores,
which have been opened in many
places throughout the country and
have made deep impression on the
people.


With every one well aware of the
great sacrifices, the tremendous cost
Of the war and the struggles which
have been going on since Hitler in
vaded Russia, the very fact that the
government has been able to open
not one but dozens of these well
stocked stores Is designed to con-
vince every Russian and his wife
that their country is the mightiest
In the world.


What other nations in the world
can do what ours Is doing?" they
ask.


Proud of Victories.


They point out proudly that Ger
mans, Romanians and Hungarians
are daily being driven from the
Soviet Union by the Russians and
the Russians alone, while the COM
bined forces of the United States
and Britain are stalled in Italy In
what the Soviet people regard as
only a minor operation.


They know meat and other things
are rationed in the United States
and Britain and that there is hardly
a citizen of those two countries who
could go out today and buy what a
citizen of Moscow can buy on the
open market.
This is very simple, very con-
vincing to the people of Russia.


just finished tour of one of
these commercial stores, as they are
called.


Prices Are High.
Prices are as high as people ex-
pected, but you can buy what you
want without coupons, ration cards.
papers, Identification or red tape
Just pick out what you want and
pay for it.
In the meat section I found beet,
mutton, pork, sucking pigs, chick
ems, geese, turkey hens, tiny deli
cate sausages and many varieties of
larger sausages and game birds.
In the fish department there were
herring, sturgeon, perch and black
and red caviar; in the dairy depart
ment, cheese, butter, condensed
milk, cream, eggs, sunflower seed,
oil and lard.


Stocks also include mushrooms,
vermicelli, rice, coffee, black bread,
white bread, -four, candies, cakes.
apples and delicacies.


As a matter of fact the stores
appear quite as well stocked as
anything one would see in Britain
or the United States before the war.


Buyers Are Radiant.


AS refreshing to see as these
foods were the expressions on
peoples faces. They were radiant,
1t Is a great comfort for them to
know the things are there If they
want to buy them.


Another morale builder was the
recent appearance of state CANDY
sellers, dressed in white coats and
white aprons, who, with neat little
trays around their necks, patrol the
streets
Candy previously had been sold
on Moscow streets, but USUALLY bv
private persons, principally women.
and prices were higher than those
OF the state vendors, whose goods
were neat and clean.
People are talking about the
clothing stores which soon are tn
open over the ceuntry, apparently
on the same basis-high prices, but
not rationed.


Along with other changes from
grim wartime conditions the entire
city has been undergoing painting,
polishing, cleaning. Buildings every
where are being spruced up.


Kremlin Being Cleaned.


The big Council of Peoples Com
missars Building in the heart of the
city Is shiny and white after weeks
OF sandblasting.


The Kremlin has been under
going refurbishing too, and little
groups of people stood by watching
as workmen cleaned the ancient
walls.


There was much happiness in the
city as tobacco and cigarette stores
threw open their doors this week.
Long, orderly lines form daily be-
fore stores that sell two packages
OF cigarettes and one large box of
tobacco to each customer.


Commercial store crowds appear
somewhat smaller now that people
seem convinced that stocks are
ample and the stores apparently
are here to stay.
Numerous children's shops have
opened, stocked by the government.


Many Kinds of Dolls.


Dolls line the shelves-from
pretty, girl dolls in various native
Russian dresses to soldier dolls in
Red Army uniforms. aThere were
coils in clown suits, animal dolls.
teddy bears, elephants, dogs and
cats.


Many stores sold big colored
sheets of paper for cutting out
paper dolls and some of these fea-
ture a Santa Claus for next New
Year Day, which is the time
Father Frost brings children
presents in the Soviet Union. But
you can't tell-Santa Claus him
self may be coming back.


At many of the stores a dozen
different games are offered, from
Gominoes to chess.


This face-lifting Is general. All
store fronts have been repaired and
sandbags have been removed. The
campaign has had a definite effect
OF raising the spirits of the people.


The revival has spread even to
apartment houses. 1 have two
friends whose elevators commenced

BY the Associated Press.


ROME, Aug. 30.-American 7th
Army troops were locked in
heavy battle today with German
forces fleeing up the Rhone VAL
ley from Southern France near
the Drome River dozen miles
north of captured Montelimar.


The Americans struck last night
while the enemy was making a
desperate effort to cross the Drome
which runs into the Rhone from
the east midway between Montelimar
and Valence.


The heaviest fighting centered
around Loriol, south of the Drom.
along Highway 7. The Germans
threw pontoons across the stream,
but whether they succeeded in get
ting any sizable group across was
not known.


Yanks Fall Back.


Meanwhile, due east near the
Italian frontier, American troops
were forced back to the outskirts OF
Briancon, city on a 4,330-foot
elevation 80 miles north of Nice. bv
an enemy force which was reported
here to have crossed into French
territory from Italy.


Whether this indicated the


flight Of any large force of Ger


man troops from Northwestern


Italy was not made clearD


The retreating German force in
the Rhone Valley. remnants of the
Nazi 10Th Army, was declared fight
ing for its very existence.


Scenes of destruction and chaos
lined the road of the enemys re-
treat. An Army spokesman said
more than 300 German vehicles, in
cluding trucks fully loaded, were
taken after the enemy abandoned
them. Two batteries of German 88s
also were taken by the pursuing
Americans.


many Germans are fleeing the
Southern France dragnet by sea in
attempts to get to Northern Italy.
The announcement said many small
boatloads of Germans had been
captured.


Prisoners Total $4,000.


Allied headquarters said the pris-
oner total had now passed $1,000,
more than 10000 being taken in the
MarSeille area alone.


At Montelimar, Rhone Valley CITY
more than 100 miles north of Mar
seille, the Americans captured Mai.
Gen. Otto Richter. the sixth German
general taken thus far in Southern
France.


The l98th Infantry Division, which
he commanded, and the 11th Pan
zer Division have both figured
prominently in all Rhone Valley
actions.


Another high-ranking German
leader to fall into Allied hands this
week was Vice Admiral Ruhfus, who
commanded the enemy defense
forces at Toulon.


Below MOntelimar American and
French troops steadily expanded the
liberated territory The French on
the west side of the Rhone Valley
reached the village of Bagnols, 13
miles northeast of Uzes.

ROME, Aug. 11.-Polish troops,
launching an infantry and tank
offensive along a emile front on
The Adriatic coast, have captured
high ground overlooking the
Cesano Valley and have sent
patrols across the Cesano River
after a 2-rnile initial advance,
Allied headquarters said today.


The towns of Scapezzano, Mon
terado and Corinaldo were seized
as the Poles swept through the Nazi
defenses. The drive to the south
bank of the Cesano put the Poles
about half way between the cap
tured port of Ancona and the next
major town of Pesara, where the
outposts of the Adriatic end of the
Gothic Line are believed to begin


Storms Fail to Halt Onslaught.


Heavy storms slowed, but failed
to halt the onslaught. Three hun
dred prisoners were taken at the
beginning of the offensive and the
Germans suffered further heavy
casualties in attempting five unsuc-
cessful counterattacks in which they
used considerable number of self
propelled guns and mortars,


The hard-pressed Germans were
reported to have withdrawn entirely
from the south bank of the Cesano.


Troops of the Polish Carpathian
Division seized important high
ground 2 miles northeast of Lacroce
after that village was taken in the
first hour of the attack.


Heavy continuous rain fell along
the entire 5th Army front and thun-
derStormS were common on most of
the 9th Army front. with the result
that activity was limited to artillery
fire and patrol actions.


Situation Unchanged in Florence.


Gen. Sir Harold Alexander's head
quarters said the situation in Flor
ence remains the same. There is
little activity apart from sniping
Our artillery continues the policy of
not Smelling the town while German
artillery fire on the southern half
of the town yesterday was less than
normal"


1t appeared that the Nazi fire was
directed primarily against roads en-
tering the town from the south.


In the bend of the Arno River
east of Florence British units occu-
pied areas south of the river from
which the enemy had withdrawn
and were within miles of the juno
ton town of Pontassieve.

The Districts 28th air-raid test
last night-the first blackout held
here since October l5-was termed
today by Army and Civilian De-
fense officials as the most sue
cessful" thus far.


Police found it necessary, how
ever, to report the names of l3
persons to the Corporation Counsel
for violating the regulations, while
5 other persons, not reported, were
given warnings.


OCD officials observed the test
from the Washington Monument.
The party included Maj. Gen. John
T. Lewis, commanding general of
the military district Of Washing
ton, and Commissioners John Rus
sell Young and Charles w. Kutz.


Gen. Lewis said he felt the black
out surpassed any previous test,
while Commissioner Young, who is
regional OCD director, termed it
highly satisfactory"


The officials were pleased with
the promptness with which street
and traffic lights went out at the
given signal.


Federal Buildings Mar Test.


Lights from several Government
buildings and passing cars were the
only factors marring the test. In
scattered instances lights in private
homes remained on, but were quickly
turned of when AFRAID wardens
noticed the violation. From the
Monument light could be seen
burning In the Capitol.


During the test the airport was
completely blacked out. Union Sta
ton was partially darkened, as al
lowed, with business almost as usual,
except during the 10-minute red
alarm period. when no one was al
lowed to leave.


Only two minor accidents, neither
involving injuries, were reported
during the blackout The actual
test lasted from $50 pm. to 10:45,
although the first audible signal for
lights-out sounded at 9:55. Tie
wavering red signal, hating pedes-
trian and vehicular traflc, came at
1920 and the second steady blast
(blue) sounded at 1890. The all
clear came at 10:45 pm.


Moonlight Is Bright.


The full moon Illuminated the
area during the test. The White
House, which had been darkened
early, was invisible to observers in
the Monument before the blackout
began, but was seen clearly after the
surrounding buildings were dark
ened


Officials were pleased at the COM
pliance of nearby counties. Arling-
ton was completely blacked out. Not
light could be seen. Frank c..
Hanrahan, Arlington County OCD
director, said, The best I've seen
yet" Excellent results also were re-
ported in Montgomery and Prince
Georges Counties.


Pedestrian traffic on downtown
streets thinned noticeably about
half an hour before the test started.


William j. Mileham, chief air
raid warden, reported his group re-
sponded "splendidly." Simulated
were held throughout the
city, but dispatching Of emergency
equipment was held to a minimum
because of the shortage of gasoline.


The blackout was the first held
under the new War Department
policy of permitting one announced
test on Sunday every three months.

LONDON, April 12.-Yugoslav

infiicting heavy casualties on the
routed garrison, including a fairly
great number" who drowned in the

Tito's communique, broadcast by

German command was rushing fresh
troops into Eastern Bosnia and

thrusts by guerrilla flying columns

vision and Chetnik troops of Gen

cessful.

German defense experts Dut also by
some of the highest Allied military lead
ers, wave of optimism swept over the
United States and Great Britain. Not
only PROFESSIONAL and political proph-
cts but men in the top military posi-
tions, such as Gen. Marshall and Gen.
Eisenhower, were confident that the
Germans would repeat their 1913 act"
and give up the struggle by the end
Of October or November of this year.


The forecasts were based on three
factors.


/. The German military leaders, rec
ognizing that there was no hope for
victory, would wish to spare the Reich's
manpower and sue for peace before
Germany suffered heavier casualties
and greater destruction.


2. The German home front would COL

g. The German armies, regardless of
how determined they were to fight to
the last ditch, could not last more than
a few months (about the end of this
year, when confronted with a COM
bined attack from the west and the east.


Expected Russian Drive.


At the time of the forecasts both Gen.
Marshall and Gen. Eisenhower were
convinced that the Russian steam roller
would be applied against the Nazis in
full strength from the east. They were
made after the Russians had started
what appeared to be their final Of
fensive from the Vistula to the Posen-
Breslau line and after severe fighting
had reached the east bank Of the
ViStula.


The Soviets had captured Praga, the
suburb of Warsaw, and were supposed
to enter the Polish capital within a
few days. The Polish underground,
commanded by Gen. Bor and taking
orders from the Allies, started their
own suicidal offensive against the we'll
armed German divisions within the city
itself in order to help the task of the
Russians.


The professional prognosticators-
newspaper and radio commentators
proved wrong. So did the men at the
head of our armed forces. We are now
faced with many more months of heavy
battle unless our Russian allies start
their winter offensive before the end
of the year.


Nothing went wrong with the Ameri-
can military operations on the western
front. They were all well conceived
and admirably executed. With the ex-
ception Of the Caen area, where there
was q costly delay, the Allied armies
went through the Germans with less
cost and greater speed than had been
anticipated originally. The divisions OF
Field Marshal Won Rundstedt and later
Won Kluge reeled under the Allied ham
mering and withdrew as quickly as
possible to their main line OF defense
on the Rhine, after losing no fewer
than o,0o0 men.


Seemed Like 1918.


The morale of the Germans began to
deteriorate, particularly within the
Reich, after the much advertised i'm
pregnable" Atlantic Wall collapsed
The plot of the reactionary old-line
German officers failed, but at the same
time it shook the morale of the home
front. Everything looked as if 1918
would be repeated, and revolutions
were expected and sometimes reported
from the usual neutral sources"


But there was an unexpected re-
vival of German morale. The Gestapo
itself could not have gotten the mil
lions of Germans back into line had
it not been for the announcement OF
the 'Morgenthau plan," which left
no hope whatever to the German pop
ulation-the very same people on whom
we had counted to bring about the
overthrow of Hitler and with it a COM
plete chaos in Germany.


The failure of the plot against Hit
Ter lined up the remaining generals
and field marshals behind Heinrich
Himmler. who today for all intents and
purpose is replacing the worn-out and
tired Fuehrer. Himmler seems to have
no illusions that he is military leader.
While Hitler Is still f1gurehead for
the masses, the actual conduct of the
internal affairs of the Reich has passed
into the hands of the Gestapo chief
while the military operations are be-
ing left exclusively to the professional
military men.


Won Rundstedt, who had been re-
tired after the Allied forces had broken
through the Atlantic Wall, is back in
command on the western front and
according to the American generals
who are facing him, is handling the
situation with more than ordinary skill.


Confidence Re-established.


Confidence has been re-established
to some degree to the German people
who believe that their West Wall will
hold against the terrific onslaught of
the Americans and their British, Cana
dilan, Polish, French and Czechoslovak
Allies.


German military leaders tell thei,
people that if they hold tight, the dis
sentions over the spolis Of war between
the Allies themselves would soon cause
a break which would profit the German
people The Germans are being told
that if they hold on. the defeat which
appeared a certainty only four months
ago may be avoided and Germany might
still come out Of this war as united
nation.


But the military factor which led Gen
Marshall and Gen. Eisenhower to predict
the end Of the war before Christmas
was the Russian offensive on the Eastern
Front. There seems to be no question
among all the military experts in Wash.

STOCKHOLM, July 1.-Allied
flags flew tonight from barri-
cades in the streets of Copen-
hagen, where $4,000 Danish pa
triots, brandishing machineguns
and rifles, were reported ready
to fight to the finish against a
German garrison of 5000 being
bolstered hourly by other troops
rushing in from Zealand.


After night of street fighting,
during which one unconfirmed re-
port said German planes machine
gunned the demonstrators, the pa
triots broke out American, British,
Russian and Danish flags and hung
them defiantly above their impro.
vised "fortresses.


The Swedish newspap per Alton
bladet quoted a report from the
underground that the demonstra-
tors-who began a general strike
yesterday-now were $4,000 strong.


Smoke Seen Over City.


Observers at Malmo, Sweden, Just
across the Orc Sound from Copen-
hagen, said smoke could be seen
rising above the city, apparently
from the bonfires started by the
demonstrators.


The general strike was described
by the free Danes as 100 per cent
effective, and as a result food sup
plies shrank, water and electricity
were cut off, and all transportation
was at Standstill.


Unconfirmed reports said more
than 700 persons had been killed
or wounded, while the free Danish
press service reported that violent
street fighting had sent 400 persons
to hospitals.


So heavy was the demand for
ambulances, the service said, that
Communicated milk trucks were
carrying the wounded away.


Demonstrators ranged through
the streets, smashing more than 100
shops which refused to join the
strike


The Germans closed the harbor
of Copenhagen today. the press

Naples, Mar. 17.-Fifth Army

corner of the town.


From that point strategic route 6,

the Liri Valley and on to Rome.

The Germans still were occupying
the ruins of ancient Mount Casino
Abbey overlooking the town and
from there were directing artillery
and mortar fire on Allied positions
in the valley.


The Germans were reported fight
ing hard to retain their hill posi-
tions west and northwest of the
town where, the communique said,
Allied forces also were making
progress.


On the beachhead below Rome
American troops beat back German
counterattacks aimed at regaining
two strong points taken two days
ago near Carano, east of Carroceto.
Casualties were inflicted on the Ger

Inside Casino Allied engineers
played major role, filling huge
bomb craters and clearing a path
through the rubble for tanks and
foot soldiers. At one point it was
necessary to build a 70-foot bridge
to permit tanks and other vehicles
to cross a water-filled obstacle.

town.

short advances, occupying several
heights not Immediately identified.

streams of shells late yesterday into
the ruins of Mount Casino Abbey,
which Is atop Monastery Hill, in
support of the ground troops climb

top, hiding activities in the valley

ALLIED HEADQUARTERS,
Naples, Mar. 14.-The weather
has improved in Italy but the
ground remains extremely soft,
holding both the Allied and Ger
man armies mudbound except
for patrol operations which yes
terday included sharp clashes
near Minturno and Casino on
the main 5th Army front, head
quarters announced today.


Allied raiders probed the German
lines around Cisterna and Littoria
in the beachhead area below Rome
and American troops seized 13 pris-
oners and dispersed the remainder
of German patrol. The British
smashed machine-gun position
and repelled a German attempt to
cross the Moletta River.


Germans Launch Attack.


The Germans launched a fairly
strong attack from three directions
against Indian positions on the 9Th
Army front last Sunday, it was an
nounced today, and fighting lasted
until the Germans withdrew. Artil-
lery, Elortars and small arms broke
up other attacks during the night.


1t was estimated that it will take
another week at least for the ground
to harden sufficiently to permit
laree-scale operations.


Allied planes flew 1000 sorties
yesterday, headquarters said, with
medium bombers pounding German
communications in Central Italy, in
Guiding rail bridges at Sarzana and
Viareggio, as well as rail yards at
Spoleto, Perugia and Fabriano.
Three enemy planes were destroyed
for loss of six Allied craft.


Rail Targets Blasted.


The Germans raided the beach,
head four times Sunday and once
Sunday night, dropping antiperson-
mel bombs, No damage was reported.


Fighter-bombers blasted road and
rail traffic south of Rome and gun
positions and supply dumps in the
beachhead area, as well as shipping
of the Dalmatian coast. Coastal
aircraft pounded docks at Santo
Stefano and rail targets at Marina
di Pisa and Montalto di Castro.
Forty-flve enemy planes were active
in the battle area yesterday.


Returning flyers said two bridges
on the west coast line, west of Sar-
zana, had been cut in the attack.
Sarzana lies east of La Spezia. Hits
were scored on the station, ware
houses and tracks and three trains
were left burning at Viareggio.

LONDON, Sunday, May 21.-The
long Eastern Front was reported
quiet through another day yes

from Moscow of mounting tension
in the Soviet capital over the pros
poets of opening a western land
front against the Germans.


Tension matching that in Britain

which emphasized that the Red
Army was eager for new offensives
of its own which would be co-ordi-
mated with blows from the west
which the Russians hope will defeat
the Germans before the end of the
year.

that there were no essential
changes on any fronts during the
day. The German command re-
ported only local fighting on the
lower Dnester, in the Carpathian
foothills and southeast of Vitebsk
to the north.

attacks near Traspol and STAN
islawow, Moscow revealed in its mid
night supplement to the commu-
nique, but were repulsed with many
losses.

Stanislawow and lost two companies
around Tiraspol, Moscow said. In
addition a similar two-day clash
southeast of Vitebsk cost the Ger
mans 200 casualties.

Yank island-hopping in the South
Pacific has produced headlines from
many battle grounds in tropical set
tings strange to American eyes.
None is more typical of the South
Seas than New Britain, exploited by
Japan from Rabaul, chief town and
key base.


A 30O-mile crescent-shaped strip
between New Guinea, bulky buffer
for Australia, and Bougainville, top
link of the Solomons chain, New
Britain provides foothold for ad-
ditional operations against the
Japs. Major targets are Jap sup
ply ships nosing through the Philip
pines and the Netherlands Indies
or dodging through the Carolines
west of Truk, enemy stronghold 1913
miles north of Rabaul.


Japanese-held since September
1912, New Britain had been admin
istered by Australia under a
League of Nations mandate issued
in 1920. Over the centuries, Span
iardS, Britons, Dutchmen and Ger
mans have had their innings in this
area, have left traces in place
names, in racial strains, in language
in political and commercial insti-
tutions.


Big as two New Jerseys, New
Britain is the largest and most i'm
portant island in the Bismarck
group. The BismarckS include New
Ireland, drumstick of land across
st. George Channel from New Brit
ain, with battered Kavieng at it's
northwestern tip; New Hanover,
and the Admiralty Islands, where
United States cavarymen riding
boats recently seized the useful
Momote airstrip on Los Negros.
Deep Valleys.


Seen from the sea, New Britain is
a forest-trimmed platform spined
with mountain ridges grading up to
mile heights, their SUBMITS shrouded
with shimmering cloud streamers
and sulphurous volcanic vapors. Deep
valleys break the line of the hills,
channel swift streams navigable in
hat-bottomed boats.


New Britain was made and shaped
by volcanic action, retains the evi-
dence in fuming cones and seething
craters. Eruptions have centered in
the eastern regions, have showered
the land with ashes, upheaved the
coastal waters, created the
box islands, wrecked craft in the
harbors, spattered shore settlements
with mud, forced evacuation of Ra-
baul and. its neighboring town,
Kokopo.


Earthquakes are fairly frequent,
shake the island from end to end,
give natives and foreigners the un-
easy feeling of sitting on huge
electric vibrator. Temperatures
rarely top 100 degrees Fahrenheit.


Civilization stops at the coast. The
interior is still pretty much of a
question mark. Many natives live
in fear of enemies and spirits, eat
ants, snakes and dogs, indulge in
noisy revelry.


Tales of cannibalism still come
from the back country, head hunt
ing persists. jungle natives live in
stockaded villages, are wary of
strangers and tribesmen from a dis
tance, believe all misfortune due to
Sorcery of enemies, are ruled by
superstitions, regard justice as IAN
eye for an eye"

TERS, June 21.-The Germans have
more rocket bomb launching in

paign of preventive Allied air at
tacks, the secret weapon" onslaught
might have been far worse, it was
disclosed at headquarters today.


Flying bombs dropped on South
ern England today, after attacks
on an increased scale during the
night, and Allied air fleets again
this afternoon assaulted the Pas-de-
Calais sector, from which the pilot
less weapons are launched.


Medium and light bombers and
fighter -bombers alone-in addition
to intermittent attacks by heavy
bombers-made 420 attacks on the
installations since January, flying
23,500 individual plane sorties and
dropping $4,000 tons OF bombs.


1t. Gen. Lewis H. Brereton, COM
manding the United States 9th Air
Force, said the rocket installations
were Of two types. The first were
built with platforms, barracks and
auxiliary buildings closely compact.
The later ones - presumably built
after the Allied attacks had begun
were widely dispersed, making
bombing difficult.


Most installations are among woods
and orchards and have been given
additional camouflage, he said, with
some buildings disguised as farm
houses.


Typical Of the setup is a long con-
crete launching platform pointed
toward England. Adjacent buildings
are used for final assembly Of the
rockets and storage.


Most of the original installations
had been put out of commission by
D-day, Gen. Brereton said, but since
the start of the bombing it has been
constant race of construction and
destruction between the Germans
and the Allied bombers.

SUPREME ALLIED HEAD
QUARTERS, Sunday, Aug. 49,
The Allies, with official mystery
cloaking the American swing
around the left flank of the half
encircled German 7th Army in
Northwestern France, pounded
forward slowly at five points in
the bulge between Mortain and
Caen yesterday and American
armor pushed toward Southern
France well below the Loire to
the portentous accompaniment
of bomb bursts on the Mediter-
ranean Coast.


One German salient six miles
wide and four miles deep was
rubbed out by coordinated British
Canadian drives below Caen.


The Germans, reversing their pre-
vious withdrawal tactics, hurled all
available reinforcements into the
Normandy bulge which American,
British and Canadian troops were
battering from three sides.


The vast regions of France below
the broad Loire River already had
been penetrated by American ground
forces which stabbed more than 10
miles southwark after liberating
Nantes.


Front Dispatches Heavily Censored.


But lack of news concerning that
front and on activity beyond LIE
Mans on the Paris road-a place
which the Americans had passed
four days previously-reached the
proportions Of complete blackout
Dispatches from the front were
heavily censored, and at the late
night headquarters press conference
there was no word of developments


The speed, extent and objectives
Of the American drives so befudled
the Germans that the Allies rigidly
continued the four-day clamp down
on word of progress, announcing,
"the situation must remain obscure
purely for security reasons"


1t asked public patience because
on secrecy depends the success of
the Allied plan and the lives of
American, British, Canadian and
other Allied soldiers"


On the remainder of the active
front, the British driving four miles
east of Thury- -Harcourt, reached
Fresney-le-Vieux and linked up
with Canadians who pushed down
from Bretteville-Sur-Laize. This
gave the British control of the
Caen- -Thury highway.


Nazi Salient Eliminated.


The Canadians took the road
junction town of Barbery and ad-
vanced mile and a half south
ward to Bois Haibout.


These drives eliminated the Ger
man salient between the Laize and
Orne Rivers. Whether any sizeable
German forces were trapped in the
area was not disclosed


East Of Bretteville, across the
Caen-Falaise road, the Canadians
advanced little over a half-mile in
the st. Sylvan area against fierce
opposition.


Southwest of Thury the British
captured st. Pierre la Vielle and
pressed on southwark within three
miles north of Conde- Noireau,
an anchor point of German po-
sitions west of the Orne.


West of Conde the British were
battling crack German troops in the
town Of Chenedolle six miles east of
Wire. The heavy fighting here as
we'll as that southeast of st. Syl-
vain involved both German SIS
troops and paratroops and the Al
lies found thickly mined each bit of
territory they were able to gain.


Americans Retake Mortain.


South of Wire the Americans re-
captured Mortain. thus adding to
the pressure on the Germans Wire
salient. but progress beyond that
bitterly contested point was slowed
by stubborn resistance.


Coming up from the south, 80
miles below the British positions,
the Americans were meeting sitter
resistance east of Mortain and
Sourdeval, field dispatches said.


Only the supreme command and
the participants knew whether the
American drive was aimed primar-
lily for Paris or to close the trap on
the German 7th Army, estimated at

To the Editor Of The Star:


Congress must not turn its back on
our merchant seamen again. For 10
long and hard years seamen have been
denied the unemployment insurance
protection afforded all other groups
CT industrial workers.


Either the House of Representatives
includes merchant seamen within the
reconversion legislation it is now form
ulating or else 1t serves notice that our
seamen are second-class citizens worthy
Of no consideration.


Our merchant seamen are tired Of
promises and recommendations that
some one else give them the protection
they seek. There Is no one else.


Who are our seamen? They are 'front.'
line fighters.


They are the men who deliver the
goods, risk the torpedoes and mines,
battle the planes and submarines, en-
dure the blackouts, crowding and ten
sion.


They are the men who have lost
proportionately four times as many men
az the armed services in the first year
Of war


They are the men who have hundreds
OF buddies in prisoner -of-war camps.
Thousands of their shipmates have
been manned. Our Congress has made
no provision for their continued care.
They are men with families which
endure the same anxieties as the FAM
lies OF our servicemen. In the absence
OF unemployment protection they and
their families may be thrown on the
beaches of hundred port cities.


And they are boys, too. They are bows
OF 1872 and II, too young to enter the
armed forces, but manning our ships.
They are boys who have as vet been
assured no education and no retraininp
on their return.


what are they asking for? Do they
csn for special privilege? Do they saw:
We who have been separated from our
homes and bear great risk deserve
special rewards? No. All they ask is
that their future be free of the un-
certainty and tension which fills their
wartime hours. They ask nothing more
than the minimum security Congress
saw mt to grant shoreside workers in
1885.

George Bill this week Merchant sea.
men must be assured UNEMPLOYMENT
insurance coverage.

IL Delayed United States Ma
rlnes attacking under cover of a
devastating naval and aerial bonn
parchment, today conquered Engebi
Island, site of the key japanese air
strip on Eniwetok Atoll, in exactly
six hours and five minutes.


1t was the quickest victory of the
Pacific war over a defended Jap
bastion.


The Jap defenders were wiped out
completely, while Marine losses were
light.


The assault on Engebi followed
the occupation yesterday of 10 small
f1anking islands without the loss of
a single life.


Attack Goes UnchalIenged.


.Battalions of the 22d Marines
under Col. John T. Walker, regi-
mental commander, swarmed onto
Engebi in the wake of battering
by naval rifles and dive-bombers
which poured more than 1000 tons
of explosives into the tiny triangular
island.


Indicative of our supremacy on
the sea and in the air is the fact
that our attack against this west
ernmost Marshall Island base, 300
miles beyond Kwajalein, was un-
challenged from the sea or by air.


went ashore with Brig Gen.
Thomas E. Watson of Washington,
commanding both the marine and
Army forces, to watch the marines
sweep across a scene of desolation
which only month ago was an
island city and the Japs most i'm
portant mid-Pacific staging area, as
well as powerful air base.


From beach to beach Engebi was
a scene of almost incredible de-
struction, not only equarng but sur
passing what was dealt to Kwaja-
lein. Not a single building was left
standing by our bombardment. Even
the skeleton structures had been
hammered down into chaotic wreck
age.


Jap Weapons Knocked Out.


Vast shell holes, uprooted defenses
and burning fuel dumps inter-
spersed the waste areas which were
strewn knee deep with shredded
palm fronds.


Engebi looked as though it had
been run over by some giant lawn
mower.


Our tremendous preliminary bonn
bardment, which rose in fury from
am. to the zero hour of the at
tack, killed many Japs and knocked
out almost all their weapons, par
ticularly those defending the
beaches.


Battleships fired against main OBJ
jectives from destroyer range, while
dive bombers dived almost to tree
top heights to lay their bombs on
specific Japanese targets.


Marine scouts under Capt. James
Jones of Joplin, Mo, the same scouts
who captured Apamama in the Gill
berts, captured 10 islands surround
ing Engebi earlier, thus preventing
a japanese escape when the full
hellfire of battleships, cruisers, de-
stroyers and carrier aircraft was
loosed against them.


Battleships Concentrate on Engebi.


While the battleships concentrated
on Engebi, cruisers and destroyers
and more dive bombers blasted our
quarry all over the Eniwetok Atoll
and did not draw the slightest
answering fire. Hellcat fighters
ranged around the atoll in flying
circus, straflng and destroying
heached landing boats and eliminat-
ing the possibility the Japanese
might shift forces from island to
island.


When the transports reached pre-
scribed areas the battleships moved
in almost to the reef


The signal bridge of this flagship
vibrated from the conclusion of the
big guns rapid-fire salvoes. Puffs of
black and greenish smoke went sky
ward from the island, flecked with
flying palm fronds.


Destroyers and cruisers meanwhile
were blasting the flanking islands
which are strung in two directions
from Engebi like pancakes on
griddle-a very hot griddle.

Broad-winged, strong flying, the eagle
leaps to his natural element-the air.

stream. There, circling with beak and
talon ready, he keeps watch.


Striding the lion, ambling the bear
side by side they enter the river. The
bear, lately having crossed many
rivers, swirns on the left. The lion,
having centuries of acquaintance with
the sea, swims on the right


Ignoring the sting of their many
wounds, shaking the water from their
coats, the bear and the lion storm the
farther bank and, having topped it,
thunder on again.


So, the three having crossed, Join
again to rid this world of their enemy.


On the nearer bank stand little frus-
trated men who marvel at this thing:
too grand for their puny souls COM
prehension. W.P.

LONDON, April 26.-American
FortresSes and Liberators, flying
in medium strength, attacked
the aircraft production center of
Brunswick and other targets in
Western Germany today with

A strong escort of Mustangs,
Lightnings and Thunderbolts, which
made up a total raiding force of
probably more than 1000 planes,

defended aircraft production center

fighter.


Some of the fighters swept air

and the crews reported heavy anti
aircraft and rocket defenses over
Brunswick. Six of the fighters failed
to return.


The Fortresses and Liberators
from Britain, carrying out their
ninth operation in the course of
12-day offensive which has been
the greatest of the war, bombed by
instrument through overcast skies,
which apparently hampered the
enemy defense.


100 Miles West of Berlin.


Brunswick, on the route to Berlin

capital, has been one of the bloodiest
targets on the books of the United
States Strategic Air Forces. Sixty
American bombers failed to return
from the daylight attack on the pro-
duction center on January IL, when
152 Nazi fighters were destroyed.


The Raj lost 38 bombers there on
January IA, and in the last attack

cans lost "a heavy bombers, while
shooting down 148 enemy aircraft.


Today's mission, the 18th this
month by the 9Th Air Force, while
employing over 1000 planes, was
considerably smaller than the 2,000-
plane armadas which have thun-
dered from Britain in daylight five
times since the huge offensive began

drive, which has scourged enemy
targets in q 750-mile arc across
Europe, rolled forward.

tinued their offensive hundreds of
lighter planes crossed the Channel

occupied territory similar to the
attacks which cost three bombers
yesterday. The explosions from
their assault were heard all the way
across the Channel.

ent Howard K. Smith In broad

out after night Mosquito squadrons

paign-and other planes sowed

flew back over Northwest Gervanyo,

ditions, the American bombers were

defense throughout the course of
their flight and were involved in
intense battles" it said

out from Britain yesterday, and the

ers were lost, along with three other

aries-and cost the Americans and

wounded on planes that returned
home after sky battles.

$50, 100000 in aircraft, probably as

amounts for bombs, fuel, main
tenance, wages and dozens of other

ANAMOSA, Iowa, Jan. 12.-Three

yesterday they would tell Gov B. B.
Hickenlooper that they were ordered
by shift captain to open the gates
through which four convicts escaped
New Year Day with the captain and
deputy warden as hostages.

Mcnamara and Donald o. Swan
son, told newsmen they were not
bringing their case to the Governor
to get their jobs back - they said
they didn't want them - but that
they felt the people had right to
know more about what happened.


The discharged guards charged
that the shift captain, Dan E.
Beam, issued an order to open the
gate through which the convicts
escaped. The opening Of the gates
was one of the factors involved in
the dismissals, based on accusations
Of violating orders.


Millsap charged his 12-gauge
pump gun, with which he usually
was equipped, was taken from him
the day of the break and that he
was given an 1886 model 10-gauge
lever action gun in its place War
den Foss Davis verified that the
pump gun had been used by his
son, who, Millsap said. went rabbit
hunting with the weapon.

1taly's great plains was absorbing
Nazl manpower at fast rate.

had never seen so many German
oeao as now ntter the bloody slopes
Of the ridges.


2,700 Prisoners Taken.


Since August 2e, when the advance
toward Rimini began, the 9th Army
has taken 2,700 prisoners in the
Adriatic sector, of whom more than
600 were Marshal Albert Kessel-
rings crack paratroopers.


Heavy rains which flooded streams
curtailed advances in the noun
famous central and western sectors
of the 9th Army front, where In
dian patrols found the enemy with
drawn from a number of villages.
The weather also hampered aerial
operations.


Sweeping close inshore the Brit
1sh destroyer HMS Loyal and the
sunboat HMS Scarab bombarded
gun positions in the Rimini area
yesterday, but spotting was difficult
because of the heavy rain.

The nonelective county boss is the
one who has really governed Mont
gomery County for the last IS years.
He has in all reality life tenure.
Through control of caucuses and
primaries under the county's pres
ent system of government he also
provides life tenures for his lieu
tenants. The proposed Montgomery
County charter and its nonpartisan
ballot and nominating machinery
make 1t possible to abolish life ten
ures.


Those who really govern under
charter are the elective council
members with four-year terms. The
charter provides no life tenures for
any one. The county manager can
be fired by the council on 80 DAYS
notice. Three department heads
the boards of education and well
fare and the health officer-have six
and four year terms under State
law.


The charter provides a merit sys-
tenn for the other three department
heads, finance, public works and
safety, and for all other employees.
They are removable under rules of
the personnel board for inefficiency
or other proper cause, but not for
political reasons. The politicians call
this life tenure. They went to bold
on to the old spoils system.


In its survey of Montgomery
County government made in 1941 on
request of the county commissioners,
the Brookings Institution said re-
garding county personnel:


Duties which require specialized
knowledge 80 are intrusted to per-
sons without the necessary qualifica-
tions. Many employees = have
been selected mainly If not ex-
clusively for political reasons.
Some positions that are unnecessary
""' have been created to pro-
vide a place on the public payroll
for party workers. = Much parti-
san work is done during official
working hours. In some instances
the evidence suggests that official
duties are largely incidental and that
the salary paid from the county
treasury Is mainly compensation for
partisan or factional activity"
Brookings adds that under such a
personnel certain citizens may be
particularly favored at public ex-
penSe whereas decisions with
respect to assessments, highways,
purchasing Of supplies, - zoning,
and SO on, should be made OBJ
jectively with judicial impartiality.


There was no surprise when the
county machine repudiated the
survey.

IRUN, Spain, Aug. 8.-Adolf
Hitler's once-vaunted Atlantic
wall, for more than 100 miles
from the Spanish frontier north
through Bordeaux, has been vir-
tually abandoned and is manned
by only a handful of over aged
German railroad troops, advices
from France said today.


These Nazi Notifications have
been outfianked to the north by
the swift progress of American
troops through Brittany and east
ward toward Paris in much the
same way as the Maginot Line was
outflanked when the Germans
broke through Belgium in 1910.


With their communications seri-
ously menaced the Germans were
said to have begun full-scale evac-
Nation of their forces in South
western France, leaving only a few
Gestapo agents and gendarmes to
cover the French-Spanish frontier.


Temporary Withdrawal.


German police at the Hendaye
bridge maintained that the evacua-
ton was purely temporary with
draWal' necessitated by the re-
assignment of border region forces
following the shift of certain SIS
ELITE Guards units of the frontier
garrison toward the Loire River.


Frenchmen living on the Spanish
side of the frontier said, however,
they are convinced the Nazi high
command is abandoning Southwest
ern France, and many believe they
will awake some morning soon and
find the last German gone.


Regular German Army forces
moved out of the region south of
Bayonne over week ago, leaving
SIS units behind The SIS forces in
turn began leaving Sunday night.


Only French customs guards and
two or three German gendarmes
were on duty at the interna tional
bridge across the Bidassoa River
here yesterday.


Artillery Being Loaded.


The German railroad troops left
behind to guard the coast were re-
ported loading the last of the Nazis'
movable artillery aboard fiat cars at
Hendaye, Bayonne and Biarritz. To
reach the German forces to the
north these guns and other supplies
will have to run the gantlet of sabo-
tagged rail lines.


Although most of the German
forces called out of Southwestern
France were rushed north to Bor-
deauX and La Rochelle, it was re-
ported some units marched by road
across Southern France toward
Montpelier and the Rhone River
Valley.


The Germans remaining on the
southwestern front apparently fear
being left behind because French
resistance forces already have sew
cred Atlantic to Mediterranean COM
munications by dynamiting rail-
roads and highways.


Railway Bridge Blasted.
AS Nazi units were being evacu-
ated northWard the Maquis dyna-
mited railway bridge north of
Bayonne Sunday night, thus cutting
a direct line to Bordeaux.


Reports circulated along the from
tier of possible Allied landings in
the Bordeaux area and on the Med
iterranean coast.


French patriots were reported
now operating around Bordeaux
and st. Jean de Luz. The Maquis
were kept out of the latter town,
which is few miles above the from
tier, by German railroad troops still
manning pillboxes there. According
to frontier reports the Tricolor al
ready is flying over the town halls
of scores of little hamlets inland
from the coast.

ADVANCED ALLIED HEAD
QUARTERS, NEW GUINEA, Sun
day, May 28.-American infan-
trymen invaded Biak Island in
the Schoutens yesterday against
strong Japanese resistance and
battled their way toward air
fields that will base Allied planes
for assaults on the Philippines.
Davas is less than 900 miles
away.


Gen. Douglas Macarthur, an
nouncing the landing today, said
the Yanks stormed the southeastern
beaches of the island after dawn
and by nightfall had established
a strong beachhead a mile east and
a mile west of Bosnik.


This vault 200 miles toward the
Philippines from Wakde Island, con-
quered only last week in another
Jump up the New Guinea coast, was
hailed Immediately by the general
as the virtual conclusion of the
Allied campaign on that huge
island.


The jungle-green-clad veterans of
other New Guinea amphibious op-
erations rushed up the sandy, gen.
tly-sioping beaches after an inten-
sive bombardment by American and
Australian cruisers.


Landing Heavily Opposed.


The landing itself was one of the
most heavily opposed of any made
by Gen. MacArthurs forces in the
Southwest Pacific theater.


The Japanese, lodged in strong
positions overlooking the beaches,
opened up with fire from heavy
mortar and automatic weapons.
Gen. MacArthur's communique
said, however, that American
losses in the operation were light.


simultaneously with the landing
enemy shore batteries carried on
q long range duel with the Amer
lean and Australian cruisers and
other naval craft. A headquarters
spokesman said minor damage and
casualties were suffered by the ma
val force.


The last report at headquarters
told Of the American infantrymen
han1rnering ahead toward the Mok-
fner, 6orido and Borokoe airdromes
2 miles away. But they were run
ming into strong enemy resistance.
Announcing the landing on Biak,
Gen. Macarthur said:


Capture Of this stronghold will
give up command and domination
OF Dutch New Guinea except for
isolated enemy positions. For strate-
gic purposes. this marks the prac-
tical end of the New Guinea cam
paign."


Appreciable Advance.


Then in special statement the
general added:


"The results of the offensive
which was launched in this theater
II month ago have more than full
filled my most optimistic hopes and
expectations. The operations have
appreciably advanced us on our
way. I am especially thankful for
our light losses. Nothing could
more clearly indicate the mercy of
a guiding providence"


Possession of Biak's three air.
fields will give Gen. MacArthurs
flyers base for blasting everything
the enemy has between New Guinea
and the Philippines.


The fields on Biak, more than 300
miles northwest of Hollandia and
200 northwest of Wakde, are within
flghter-escorted bomber range of a
nest of Japanese airfields on Noem-
foor and Japen Islands and the
enemy mainland bases of Manok-
wari, Nabire and Babo. .


The landing at Biak places Gen.
Macarthur virtually as near to the
Philippines as to his main New
Guinea base at Finschaffen.


Heavy Aerial Softening.


The Biak invasion was preceded
by one of the heaviest aerial soft
enings ever handed a japanese New

islands largest village, was ablaze.

ceding night when, an RAF COM
mentator estimated, at least 100

The fight for custody OF 6-year-

give his decision this afternoon.

and his grandmother, Mrs. Susie
j. Gilboy, finished their cases to-
day. Both women seek the child's
custody.


A habeas corpus proceeding, insti-
tuted by the boys mother, began yes
terday. The mother is the widow
of Army Warrant Officer John w.
Worthington, who was slain last

rant officer, Carl Moulinie. was con-

teenth street NV, contends her
child, who was 6 yesterday, has

grandmother. Mrs. Gilboy claims

ington had failed to take proper care

had asserted sometime before the
shooting that she wished Worthing-
ton would commit suicide so she

give details of the killing because of

The battle of Leyte was practi-
cally halted by bad weather to-
day while Manila recovered from
its fourth major American air
raid of the month.


On Leyte, typhoon took prece-
dence over efforts of both sides on

MacArthur's communique noted
that the 32d Division was making
some progress near Limon, reported
that the enemy was continuing des-
perate efforts to break road block
south of the town-and added, sig
nificantly. "all traffic. air, ground
and sea, is fraught with great diff
culties and hazards: and battle con-
ditions are becoming static"


Only in the air was there spec
tacular activity. There, 35 enemy
fighters and dive bombers raided
American positions, losing seven air.
craft to air patrols and ground fire.
American aircraft countered with
attacks on japanese communica-
tions lines, supply areas and water
front targets near Ormoc.


Manila Airfields Damaged.


Vice Admiral John S. McCain's
carrier planes hit Manila again Sat-
lurday, damaged airfields, set blazes
haring on three merchant ships and
destroyed lib Japanese planes. Most
/ of these were on the ground. Only
10 enemy planes were shot down in
the Manila area and another near
the fleet carriers


Admiral Chester w. Nimitz an
nounced the raids at Pearl Harbor
last night. The announcement made
no mention of damage to American
planes or ships (although Radio
Tokyo said nine American aircraft
were downedD, nor of additional
japanese shipping in the Manila
area. This was surprising, in view
|of the recent japanese attempts to
reinforce Leyte by sea.


Morrie Landsberg, Associated
Press war correspondent, reported
from Admiral McCain's flagship that
American pilots found "a ghost
fleet" of 100 war-crippled japanese
ships" in Manila harbor and few
targets worth attacking.


Counterattacking japanese planes
which escaped the antiaircraft bar
rage over the task force went home
without dropping their bombs, Mr.
Landsberg said. He listed eight
more enemy planes shot down than
Admiral Nirnitz reported and five
oil-laden luggers blown up off the
southern Luzon coast.

Schaffhausen Saturday and assur-

number of other sections of Switz-

the bombing of Schaffhausen, ap-

are effective since the violation of
the air of neutral territory con-
tinues.

Americans occurred over the week.
end, although the Swiss people gen.
orally showed their characteristic
restraint.

and escaped prisoners of war re-
ceived instructions to avoid bars
and public places, to eat at restau-
rants only if necessary and to leave
Immediately after they were fin-
ished, and to continue normally but
apologetically their relations with

BUENOS AIRES, Mar. ia 49,
year-old Argentine woman gave
birth yesterday in a Buenos Aires
suburban hospital to quadruplets
three of whom died after a few
hours.


The multiple birth occurred while
veriflcation still was being sought
for the previously reported birth OF
qu1ntuplets to a well-to-do Argen-
tine rancher and his wife.


A baby girl, weighing about 2
pounds, was the only survivor of the
quads-two boys and two girls
born to Sonora Cello Giachino de
Angiulli.


Reporters, meanwhile, failed to
find any registration of the birth Of
quintuplets here, although Argentine
law makes parents responsible for
registration of births within three
days.


The quints were reported to have
been born to Senior and Sonora
Franco Diligenti eight months ago
and kept secret because the parents
wished to avoid public curiosity.


The Buenos Aires Herald first re-
ported the birth of the quints, and
Senor Diligenti has told newsmen
their names are Maria Fernando,
Maria Esther, Franco, Maria Chris
tina and Carlos.

PORT BOU, Spain. July 10
French patriot organizations have
turned their energies against the
Germans dwindling fuel supplies
throughout France, destroying gas
oline, oil and coal already stored or
en- route to dumps and sabotaging
mines and production plants, border

This is only the beginning" de-

league with the patriots. I'VE plan

power the Germans have is their

LONDON, June 14.-Red Army
troops have advanced to within
80 miles of the important port of
Viipuri, crushing Finnish troops
resisting from strongly fortified
positions, Moscow announced
today, and enemy reports said
Russia's whole northern front,
from the Arctic to the White Sea
and Gulf of Finland, was ablaze
with action.


Finnish and German radio broad
casts declared the Russians were at
tacking in the Lisa sector between
the Arctic ports of Murmansk and
Petsamo, and Berlin asserted Soviet
forces also were striking southwest
of Narva in Estonia.


/ Finnish Strong Points Taken.


In addition, the broadcasts said
there was reconnaissance activity
! in the Kandalaksha sector on the
shore of the White Sea, $50 miles
northwest of Viipuri, and near
Loukhi, on the railway from Arch
angel across Finland to the Gulf of
Bothnia.


The Moscow communique was re-
stricted to the Karelian Isthmus
fighting, saying Soviet troops cap
tured several Finnish strongpoints
during yesterdays battling and list
ing five in the area of Kivennappa
taken Monday.


The Russians are within 20 miles
of the Mannerheim Line, main de-
fense barrier across the Karelian
Isthmus, Moscow bulletins indicated
after clearing the second belt of
approaches.


Natural Defense Obstacles.


Finnish advices relayed through
Stockholm said stout resistance was
confronting the Russians in the
Kivennappa sector with the YAM
melsuu River front still intact. Be-
hind Kivennappa there is hilly
country and many small lakes, and
on the eastern side of the isthmus
marshland about 20 miles long and
3 to 4 miles wide presents a natural
obstacle.

ROME, Sept. 2. - Hard driving
American 7th Army troops drove on
Lyon tonight after capturing the
Rhone Valley town of Vienne, IA
miles to the south.


Earlier 1t. Gen. Alexander M,
Patch's Americans had thrust
quickly through the village of
Beaurepaire, 80 miles south of Lyon.


The official announcement of the
latest gains declared action has
been linked largely to enemy de-
fense of road blocks and patrol
clashes"


Nowhere in Southern France was
any German unit still attempting a
determined stand, and even the
rear guards were losing heart as
the threat of being cut off from
escape to the Reich grew steadily
with the advance of other American
forces toward the German and
Swiss frontiers.


On the west side of the Rhone
River French columns continued
mopping-up operations and passed
Montfaucon and Torunon, both
more than 40 miles below Lyon.


Earlier observation had shown
that the enemy was digging some
defensive positions around Lyon,
presumably in the hope of slowing
the American pursuit. Swiftness
Of the advance, however, might
cause the Germans to relinquish
Lyon without real fight for that
principal Rhone Valley dty and
famous silk center.


During the day it was an
nounced that prisoners taken by
the 7th Army now exceeded $1,000,
and that in their eastern tanning
out maneuver along the Mediter-
ranean they had occupied Contes,
eight miles northeast of Nice.


Movement of the Americans in
the area north of Grenoble, from
which they could bypass Lyon and
get astride the German northward
escape routes, remained officially
vague. The mornings communique
said only that some American ele-
ments were beyond Voiron," which
is 43 miles southeast of Lyon, but
mentioned no distances.

German Staff Buried.


Other troops moving in from

center of interest. AS recently as

in Normandy, the entire picture was
transformed, and so reaching

MADRID. July diplomatic re-
ports reaching Madrid today indi-
Gated the Germans may wipe out the
last pretense OF Vichy independence
within the next week, assume all
civil functions themselves, and turn
France into a full-fiedged puppet.


Available information suggested
the vichy government already was
In process Of liquidation in series
Of meetings between Germans and
collaborationist leaders.


The pattern was reminiscent of
the fate of such countries as Hun
gary and Romania, where the Nazi
sword became absolute as the con-
quering Russian armies rushed for
ward. In the case of France the
Allied beachhead in Normandy,
the strong resistance movement
throughout the country and the fear
of new Allied landings may con-
tribute to similar action.


The reports reaching here said the
Vichy MINISTRIES Of the interior,
justice and propaganda probably
would be handed over bodily to the
Naz.s. and all Vichy courts would
cease functioning. leaving all cases
to German military courts.


The propaganda ministry may al
ready be fully in the hands of the
Germans. The Vichy radio skipped
its usual news broadcasts yesterday
morning without explanation. but
come on the air later with a re-
vamped program paralleling Ger
man domestic programs.


The Federal Communications
Commission noted other changes in
French broadcasting yesterday. The
FEC said the Vichy Telegraph Agen-
cy transmitted no press dispatches,
giving the explanation that material
had mot yet arrived" On the other
hand. the Paris radio announcer,
after broadcasting the German COM
munique. read it second time to
permit the press to take 1t down.

was omitted during the day, the

CLEVELAND, May 1l.-Workers
who are forced into lower-paid jobs
when the shifting needs of war pro-
duction affect their plants cannot
continue to draw their former wage
rate, the region War Labor Board
ruled today.


The boards decision involved a
request of the CIO United Auto
Workers that 80 welders at the Twin
Coach Co., Kent, Ohio, be paid
welders' rates despite the fact the
company had exhausted its welding
contracts and the men we're working
at other jobs.


The union contended the company
had promised duration jobs" to the
welders and asked that the welding
rate of $1.25 an hour be continued
while the men were performing
other work rated at $1.15 an hour.
The board ruled that the issue of
any company promise did not con-
stitute a wage stabilization question,
but that payment of the higher rate
while the men were not working as
welders violated wage stabilization
policies.


Also denied was the unions re-
quest that the employees be reim-
bursed for time and expense in
volved In their original training as
welders. However, the WLB directed
the company to increase the hourly
wage rates of 40 assistant foremen
by one and one-half cents to elm
mate intra-plant inequities' and to
place them on scale 10 per cent
above the highest-rated employees
they supervise.

instantly became close friends, and
now boast there since has never

them.

Watson, have featured the famous

GEN. MACARTHUR'S HQ. IN
NEW GUINEA, May (INS)-
Japans tottering island bases
north of Australia rocked today
under widely separated assaults
by heavy bombers of the u. s.
Fifth Air Force which struck
more than 700 miles west of cap
tured Hollandia in Dutch New
Guinea.


A communique reported that
American invasion forces had ex-
tended their grip throughout the
Hollandia area and captured the
Tami airdrome, Il miles east OF
Humboldt Bay.


WIDE BOMBINGS


Liberator and Mitchell bombers
of the Fifth Air Force blasted
Jap positions i'm western New
Guinea with nearly 80 tons OF
explosives. Air fields, ground in
stallations and gun positions
were raked in the Sorong area,
Shouten Islands. and Wakde area.


Other Liberators hit Mokmer
airdrome on Biak Island in the
Shouten group 100 miles east OF
Manokwari. Fifteen parked planes
were wrecked and fuel fires
started.


Twelve Jap fighters attempted
interception. Three were shot
down and two others listed as
probably destroyed.


BLAST SUPPLY LINES


Liberators and Mitchells blasted
Jap supply and defense areas on
Wakde Island and the Sarni
coast. American naval units in
night bombardment poured IS
tons OF shells into the same area.


Attack planes scattered S5 tons
Of explosives over Jap positions
at Wewak in British New Guinea.
At Nightingale Bay night naval
patrols accounted for 100 Jap
casualties as they sank six troop
laden bargcs.


Medium and light bombers from
Solomons bases maintained the
relentless aerial pressure on Ra-
haul, blasting Rapopo, Vunakanau,
and Vunapope airdromes.

The old Roman road from Cologne on
the Rhine to Boulogne on the English
Channel, crossing Belgium from Wise

kirk, is the line that has always divided
Dutch-speakngSFlemings of the poppy

More exactly, the Flemings speak

Flemings and Walloons


The Walloons, their culture centered

Flemings, slow. persistent, thorough.
Both groups were leaders in the first
colonies of New York, New Jersey. Penn

duced masters in arts and letters.

Flemings and Walloons may exploit
their own differences, but outsiders may
not exploit them. Germany's propa-
gandists, seeking repeatedly to breach
the nation have found that Belgium
comes first with both Flemings and
Walloons.


Five Biggest Cities


Included in the nine provinces that
form Belgium are five large metropolitan
centerS. Brussels, centrally situated
capital, counts a million people in it's
cluster of Is communities. From Brus-
sells, trade routes lead to four centers,
one for each direction of the compass,
each with over 400 900 community pop-
ulation. These are Antwerp, north:
Liege, east; Charleroi, south; Gent, west.


Brussels, where the Flanders plain
breaks into low, rolling hills, has often
been called Europes little Paris" It's
devotion to art and fashion, it's parks,
boulevardS and quaint evidences of
earlier days convey that impression and
hide its industries-textile factories,
foundries, machine shops, sugar re-
ineries. 1t was the center of the 1880
revolt that separated Belgium from the
present territory of the Netherlands.
During the first World War the city
was the scene of the execution of Nurse
Edith Cavell. The two German in
vasions of the last quarter century
spared most of its landmarks, but de-
stroyed its industries and deported its
laborers.


The Port of Antwerp


Antwerp, so miles up the Schelde from
the sea, is Belgium's great port with
one of Europe's best harbors Cutting
diamonds, imported from the Belgian
Congo, making textiles and cigars have
been important Antwerp industries.


Liege, is Belgiums fortified arsenal on
the Meuse. The Albert Canal makes the
city virtually seaport.


Charleroi and its satellite towns are
at the heart of Belgium's coal and iron
mining region that reaches from Mons
to Liege. Iron and steel mills, railway
shops, glass and hardware factories dot
this region of underground resources.


Gent, soul of Flanders, with 200
bridges spanning its canals and island
dotted streams. stands at the junction
OF the Leie Gys) and the Schelde. Cot.

ALLIED HEADQUARTERS,

beachhead below Rome were

stab weakly at the Allied lines
after the failure of their latest

A dusk assault against American

filtration attempts in the Moletta

beachhead. Three German divisions
had previously been identified
in the assault, but the Allied COM
mand later learned the crack Her.
mann Goering Panzer Division and
the 715th Infantry also were en-
ployed. The latter outfit suffered
heavy casualties in both of the last
two offensives.
