LONDON, Jan. 7.-American
Marauder bombers smashed at
military objectives in Northern
France today, keeping the
round-the-clock offensive roll
ing after Raj Mosquitoes raided
Western Germany last night for
the 9Th night in succession.


The Marauders returned from
their cross-Channel sweeps in early
afternoon without single loss. The
medium bombers were a part of the
parade of Allied fighters and fight
er-bombers observed streaking across
toward the French coast shortly
after the Mosquitoes returned from
their night raids.


The fleet plywood bombers re-
turned without loss at the hands of
German antiaircraft defenses or
night fighters, an Air Ministry COM
munique said


Northern France Also Hit.


In addition to bombing objectives
in Germany, the identity of which
was not disclosed, the Mosquitoes last
night also stabbed at Northern
France and other RAF planes laid
mines in enemy waters, the bulletin
declared


Apparently considerable num-
ber of the hardhitting Mosquitoes
participated in the operations, for
observers on the British southeast
coast reported last night that they
| had heard outward bound planes
passing overhead for almost two
hours.


The Mosquito raids were accom-
panied by air alerts in Geneva and
other Swiss cities, the German-con-
trolled Paris radio said.


Diversionary Raid on Berlin.


The previous night the Mosquitoes
staged diversionary raid on Berlin,
causing the Germans to rush their
night fighters to the defense of the
capital while great fleet of British
heavy bombers pounded the Baltic
port of Stettin with more than 1000
tons of bombs almost unopposed.


Stockholm dispatches said an
eyewitness to the Stettin raid
said he heard reports in the city
that 1000 persons had been killed.
The traveller said extensive
damage was done to the harbor
area, an important feeder line to
German forces in Finland and
along the Baltic front.


(The newspaper Morgon It'd
ningen had reported earlier that
10000 persons were left homeless.)


Yesterday, the Air Ministry said,
Raj light and medium bombers
teamed up with fighter-bombers to
attack military objectives in North
ern France. The light and medium
bombers were escorted by Allied
fighters.


RAF, Dominion and Allied fighters
also carried out supporting sweeps,
the ministry, said.


From the daylight operations six
Allied aircraft were reported miss
ing. Three enemy planes were shot
down.


Fighters Set Record.


American Thunderbolt and Light
ming fighter planes which escorted
heavy bombers in Wednesdays as
sault on the German U-boat and
shipbuilding center of Kiel destroyed
ID Nazi aircraft without loss for a
new American fighter record over
Germany. The previous record
was 16.


The United States Air Force an
nouncement today said the fighters
were led by Maj. James r. Howard
Of st. Louis.

LONDON, Aug. 30.-American
heavy bornbers, anti-aircraft fire
and fighter pilots all were directed
against German robot bombs which
kept hurting the Channel toward
London and Southern England.


One pilot shot down three before
dusk. Ground fire brought down
many more. The heavy bombers
attacked launching platforms in
Northern France.


Flight 1t. Rene Van Lierde, =
Belgian. has bagged ~ bombs 50
far; another pilot has 50 and
Pole has down 20. Many Of the
pilotless explosives have been de-
stroyed by American flyers who have
spotted them by chance while on
other missions.


Robots Fall During Night.


New waves Of flying bombs
dropped during the night, most Of
them apparently coming from the
region west of Boulogne, toward
which Allied armies now are rapidly
advancing.


The attacks ended q lull which
had continued for two successive
nights-a break believed due in part
to German dimculties in transport
ing the robots to launching sites.


During the night attack the
southeast coast town Of Folkestone
shook and the earth rumbled to
a distant explosion which some re-
ports said was the heaviest shock
felt there during the entire war.


May Have Been Test.


Most persons agreed that the ex-
plosion, shortly before midnight,
occurred across the Channel in
France and there was some belief
that the Germans might have
been testing their long g-threatened
vengeance weapon No. T."


Meanwhile a Stockholm dispatch
reported that all German papers
had carried cryptic article by Elite
Guard War Reporter Joachim Fer
nau who wrote that German victory
was not only sure but very near
apparently an attempt to bolster
secret weapons still to come.


Despite heavy Allied bombing the
Germans are directing most of their
robot attacks from the Pas de Calais
area across the Channel.

STOCKHOLM, Feb. 23.-The
Swedish Telegraph Agency said to-
day that Russian lettering had been
found on bomb fragments at
Straengnaes. 40 miles west of Stock
holm, after a small number of for
eign planes dropped explosives there
and on the capital last night.


Signal lights, indicating they we're
trying to land, also were dropped
by the planes, and it was believed
possible that they were damaged
craft which jettisoned their ex-
plosives before attempting emer-
gency landings.


Russian bombers raided Turku,
on the west coast of Finland $50
miles from Stockholm, earlier last
night.


Bombs Hit Summer Theater.


Several Of the bombs which fell
in Stockholm crashed directly into
a summer open-air theater, in the
only extensive open area in the
southern section of the city. No
casualties were reported, but hun
dreds Of windows were said to have
been shattered.


A Swedish communique identified
the aircraft, which came from the
east, only as foreign planes" The
number of planes involved was
placed officially at three, but private
reports said there were 10. One was
said to have crashed near Stock
holm, but it had not yet been found,
and there were no other reports of
crashes or emergency landings.


The Swedish home guard was
alerted, but air-raid sirens were not
sounded.


The newspaper Aftonbladet said
today that gunfire off the southeast
coast of Sweden's Aaland Islands in
the Gulf of Bothnia was heard for
six hours during the night.


Finnish Cities Reported Raided.


Fresh reports on the nights
strange activities said 20 foreign
planes, fully lighted, flew over Umea,
275 miles north of Stockholm on the
Gulf of Bothnia.


There were strong indications sew
eral Finnish cities were raided dur
ing the night; which might account
for the air activity over Sweden.
Finland announced only that Turku,
on the west coast, was bombed and
an alarm sounded in Helsinki.


Aftonbladet's Berlin correspond
ent said news of the bombing Of
Stockholm created something of a
sensation in the German capital.
The correspondent said private cir
cles took the view that the Rus
slams had attacked the city, trying
to provoke Sweden, which carries
on an extensive iron ore traffic
with GERMANY.

WITH THE AMERICAN CON-
MANDO FORCE ON THE BURMA
BORDER, March % Delayed -
American Air Commands in gliders
have made new and daring land
Ing deep inside Burma-this time to
carry assistance to British column
battling its way through the jungle
without supply support.


A train of gliders commanded by
Maj. William Taylor, jr.. 1925 Kill
bourne place NV, Washington.
D. c., sailed down beside the British
at dawn. bringing not only soldiers
but heavy machinery with which to
build a runway suitable for the
landing OF transports with supplies


The British force had been march
ing steadily for many weeks across
rivers, over mountains and through
Jungles, penetrating more than 100
miles into Japanese-occupied terri
tory, and needed ammunition and
food before further clashes with the
enemy.


Road Machinery Asked.


From somewhere in that wilder
ness came a message to Col. Philip
Cochran, asking if his gliders could
bring road-making machinery so
that transports could land.


Within a few minutes Col. Coch-
ran notified Maj. Taylor to prepare
glider force as soon as possible.


Glider Pilot 1t. Jackie Coogan,
former film star, heard the CONVEX
Sation and called two other glider
pilots, 1t. Steve Thomas Umipskl.
Maiden, Mass, and 1t. Neal J..
Blush, Whitefish. Mont. They came
on the double along with 1t. Pat
rick Hadsell, Denton, Tex.


Without asking where they were
going, the pilots volunteered to go
with Maj. Taylor on the mission.
While these four went off to pre-
pare their gliders, other pilots of
the motorleSs craft were called in
for briefing.


Ready AZ Hours Later.


Forty EIGHT hours later in the
darkness before dawn the train of
gliders with machinery were being
towed over the 1000 oot-high Chin
Mountains into Burma.


In addition to Maj. Taylor and
his four original volunteers, pilots
and co-pilots of the gliders were
Its. Soloman Schnitzer, Port Ar
thur, Tex; Vincent j. Rose, Ke-
nosha, Wis; Richard Kuenstler. San
Antonio, Tex; James Sever, Nor
folk, Va, and Flight Officers Ben
jamin o. Lavender, Wichita Falls.
Tex, and James S. Bartlett, Lucas,
Kans.


At the first light of day the
gliders cut loose from the transports
and with their heavy loads almost
dove down into field. making good
landings, while the British troops
gaped and cheered from the edge
of the jungle.


Maj. Taylor, leader of the glider
train, was the first to bring his craft
down. Soldiers rushed out as each
glider landed and pushed it under
the trees, where it was quickly I'M
loaded.


Landing Strip Ready In Day.


A day later the landing strip was
completed and the radio called for
the transports. That night scores
of transports with war supplies
landed by the aid of makeshift
field lights.


When the transports were un-
loaded, the gliders were rushed into
place behind the planes and one by
one the gliders were pulled of the
field and back to their base.


This operation behind the enemy's
lines was considered one of the most
successful transportation operations
yet attempted.


Members of the same glider COM
mand of Col. Cochran made SIM
ilarly spectacular landing in North
ern Burma March to hgelp British
Indian airborne troops launch an
offensive from the Japanese rear
The announcement, made March 49,
called it the largest aerial offensive
operation of the war.

Psychic bids are dangerous not
alone because the partner frequent
ly does not know how to interpret
them, but sometimes because of the
holdings of the adversaries who are
able to take advantage of such q
call. An illustration occurred in a
Federal Bridge League game. West
was dealer. He held four spades
to the ten spot, three hearts to the
nine, four small clubs and the ten
and one diamonds.


The North hand had king and one

heart, queen and two small clubs
and six diamonds to the jack, queen
and ace The South hand had ace
and one small spade, two small
hearts, ace, king. queen and two
clubs and the king, nine and two
small diamonds. North doubled,
and East, having nothing valuable
except the king, queen and four
hearts, passed. South called two no
trump. North then bid four no
trump, and South jumped to six
no trump, recognizing that West
had opened psychic.


West led the ten of diamonds,
which was won by South's king, who
then cashed his ace and king of
spades and ran five more diamonds,
discarding heart and club. Aft
er winning with the ace of hearts,
all OF his clubs were good, and he
claimed a grand slam against the
psychic bid. Had West passed origi-
nally, North would have bid the
diamonds and, although slam was
possible in that suit, it probably
would not have been bid. In any
event, it would not have counted
for as much as the slam in no trump.
Some of the players at other tables
even stopped at five diamonds.

In the opening hours of the attack

A steady rain, however. turned open

fires shot down three Focke-Wulfe
1905 out of six over the beachhead

British Wellingtons were thrown

tanks near Ponte Rotto.


The Germans constantly shelled

height of the attack Tuesday.


Allied artillery broke up small
scale German diversionary attack
Tuesday about 2 miles due south o1
Cisterna and total of Ill prisoners

An Allied counterblow wiped out
small enemy gains. In the same
general area, southwest of Littoria

oners from a Nazi patrol of 80 tc

In the gullies and caves of the
Upper Moletta River sector south

cessful encounters, it was an
nounced. There a British tank
force, piercing the German lines al
dawn Tuesday, entered small set
tlement, shot up an enemy platoon
then retired.

fronts

ing the enemy was kept up else
where besides the beachhead. Raj

ALLIED HEADQUARTERS, Ma
pies, May 1.-Six Italian youths
who crossed the lines into Allied
occupied Italy to spy for the Ger
mans have been executed by a firing
squad after a tried, Allied head
quarters announced yesterday.


They were Giorgio Tapoli, Vim
cenzo Tedesco and Brabci Ascgue.
rulm, each 18; Idalo Palesse and
Enrico Menicocci, both 20, and Ma
rino Cantelli, 81.

from the Germans to cross the lines
to get military information, such
as gun positions. One was charged
with getting political and economic
information and two were given
sabotage jobs, as well as espionage,
and carried delayed action incen-
diary bombs, headquarters said.

Unless the alcoholic realizes that he is sick.

devsing of methods of control and rehabilitation.

cure" has been found for excessive drinking.
This is never true, for there is specific remedy
for helpless dependence upon alcohol in the sense
that there is cure for diphtheria, or in the
that there are definite means for controlling the
consequences of diabetes.


There can be cure for alcoholism The treat.
ment must be fitted 10 the cause.


There are however, various ways and means
by which the problem drinker be helped 10
overcome his habit, provided always that he wants

CHUNGKING, Sept. 1.-THE
Chinese high command an
nounced today the recapture Of
Tengchung from the Japanese,
saying this marks another high
point in the effort to clear the
area west of the Salween River
and removes another obstacle to
reopening the Burma road"


The fall Of the city, held by the
Japanese for more than two years
and once their Yunnan Province
headquarters, was significant gain
in the first real Chinese offensive in
more than seven years of war.


1t was four months and three days
ago that the Chinese, aided by
American elements and the United
States 14th Air Force, opened the
Salween push. Clearing of Teng-
chung goes far toward accomplish
Ing the purpose of the offensive
to reopen the Burma road in China,
join with Gen. Joseph w. Stilwell's
forces in Northern Burma and open
the land supply route to blockaded
China.


Chinese Trained by Yanks.


Tengchung is IS miles from the
Burma border and IS mines west OF
the Salween River bridge.


The Chinese troops, commanded
by Marshal Wei Lin-huang, were
trained and equipped by an Ameri-
can force under Brig. Gen. Frank
Dorm, which has been advising and
assisting the Chinese throughout
the campaign


Before the Chinese can effectively
use the Burma road they must wipe
out the remaining opposition imme-
diately west of the Salween Bridge
and eliminate the Japanese from
the Lungling and Mangshih areas.


A high command communique
said japanese hospital patients cap
tured at Tengchung Tuesday re-
ported the besieged garrison had
been without food for four days.


Wounded Aided Defense.


A captured japanese veterinary
officer was quoted as saying that
all the lightly wounded and one
third of the more seriously wounded
Japanese were in the defense lines
at the time he was seized.
The high command announced
that enemy troops captured a hill
3 miles north of Lungling Tuesday
and thus extended their lines across
the Lungling- -Tengchung road, but
said that the pressure of the REIN
forced japanese in THIS area de-
clined somewhat yesterday.

text:
PHots overcome tremendous obstacles to
fly "over the hump" Their heavily loaded
transports must climb $4,000 feet in IS min
utes to get over the first pass between the
hve-mile-high mountains.


That climb is like walking from the inside
of roaring oven into winter day in the
Yukon. At take-off, the thermometer registers
1lO' in the shade, and the fliers have to wear
gloves so they won't burn their fingers on the
controls The only other things they wear ars
socks, shoes and shorts.


25' Below "Over the Hump"


At 5000 feet it gets little cool and the
pilots pull on their pants At $4,000 it begins
to get really cold and the feece-lined suit goes
on. Even then, there's plenty of shivering in
the ~ to Is below zero temperatures.


After the first ridge is passed, the ATc
pilots must keep their Pratt & Whitney-pow-
cred transports flying at 16,OOO-feet altitude
or more for the rest of the 500-mie trip That
means the pilots are on oxygen six hours
out of seven on the round trip between India
and China.


For the eight long months of the monsoon
season they fly mostly on instrument, because
the weather is really thick But they fly. They,
fight some of the most vicious air currents
in the world amid the jumbled Himalayas.


All Supplies Go In By Air


Everything imaginable goes into China
by air - gasoline, bombs, jeeps, artillery,
rifles, ammunition, clothing, aircraft engines. ]
spare parts and food, in quantities which,
dwarf the IS 900 tons a month formerly
carried over the Burma road. On return trips,
tungsten, mica and other vital materials are
flown out, in addition to military PERSONNEL


On the grueling run, Douglas Skytrains
and Skymasters, Consolidated Liberator Ex-t
presses and Curtiss Commands are used.
All are powered by Pratt & Whitney enginess
The Skytrains, Skymasters and Liberator Ex.
presses are equipped with Hamilton Standard
Hydromatic propellers.


The India-C China air route was opened less
than month after the fall of Burma. II
started with handful of veteran Douglas
Skytrains, Army version of the familiar
DC-3 commercial transport. There were few
pilots, almost no servicemen. Operations be-
gan from single landing strip. There were
no dispersal areas for air raid protection.
Servicing was done in the open. Crews loaded
their own airplanes. Flying the uncharted,
little-known route, pilots felt their way over
the mountains and jungles to China.


More Planes and Pilots Arrive


A month later more Skytrains came. Addi-
tfonal pilots came from the domestic airlines
and the American Volunteer Group. Things
were beginning to move.


The real expansion began early in 1o43,
when the 1ndia-China lifeline was put into
the hands of the Air Transport Command and
new transports like the Curtss Commando,
Liberator Express and Douglas Skymaster
with their large capacities were put into ser.
vice.

SAN SALVADOR, Ell SALIVA
DOR, April 15.-Official reports to-
day said So persons were killed and
134 wounded in the abortive revolt
here two weeks ago.


The reports, among the first since
the Palm Sunday rebellion, said 10
leaders of the revolt had been exc
cuted after a court martial


A fire which broke out during the
revolt destroyed two square blocks
in the center of San Salvador, in
cluding the handsome casino.


These official reports did not
give the cause of the fire, but
travellers arriving in Panama
and Nicaragua said 1t started
when rebel pilots attempted to
bomb the barracks of the police,
who remained loyal to the gov
ernment of President Maximili-
ano Hernandez Martinez)


Executed Leaders Identified.


Police Department reports on the
dead and wounded identified them
carefully and told where the bodies
were. The army, reporting on the
executions of the leaders, said their
courtmartial began April 9. After
each spoke in his own defense, the
report said, they were sentenced to
death at am. April 10 and shot
the same morning.


Those executed included Gen. AL
fonso Marroquin, commander of the
first infantry regiment; Col. Tito
Tomas Calvo, named as the leader
of the revolt, and number of sub
ordinate officers. There was still
nothing official on the fate of the
civilian participants.


Two Radio Stations Seized.


The official reports said the rebels
seized two radio stations about noon
Sunday. April 2, announced that
the president had been overthrown
and called the populace to a mass
meeting at $3.50 pm. The populace,
fearing further shooting, stayed
home while rebel planes flew over
the city.


The president, who had been out
Of the city, returned and took COM
mand of the police. Rebellious
soldiers were beseiged in their bar
racks until Monday afternoon, when
they surrendered. The planes,
meanwhile, had lost their base when
police seized the airf1eld. Some
flyers used their remaining gasoline
to flee the country, others landed
and were made prisoners.

LONDON, Sept. 30.-Nearly 1000
American and British bombers and
fighters closed out one of their
biggest months today by plastering
five German synthetic oil plants and
rail centers in the industrial Ruhr
and Rhine valley beyond the Allied
land armies.


In three separate waves more than
800 American Flying Fortresses and
Liberators. escorted by TOO fighters,
hammered choked freight yards at
Munster, Hamm and Bielefeld,
which feed the embattled German
frontier troops A small force of
American hea'vyweights also at
tackled a Nazi ordnance depot at
Bielefeld.


A communique from the United
States Strategic Air Forces reported
that 10 bombers were lost on this
mission, but that all fighter craft
returned safely.


Raj Switches to Day Raid.


Munster, the capital of West
phalia, and Bielefeld are important
rail and communications centers,
while Hamm is site of Germany's
largest freight yards.


RAF Halifaxes and Lancasters.
switching from night duty, raided
Bottrop and Sterkrade, a few miles
northwest of Essen, the sites of
already partially destroyed syn
thetic oil plants producing almost
solely for Nazi Army needs. A
good-sized force of RAF Spitfires
and Mustangs escorted the big
British bombers, one of which was
lost.


Last night a force of RAF Mos
quitoes attacked karlsruhe, concen-
trating their bomb loads with the
aid of good visibility, while others
laid mines in enemy waters. None
was lost.


Flyers Ignore Bad Weather.


Today was the sixth successive
day that the Allied bombers were
over the Western Reich, beating up
transportation links to the front.
and the fifth out of six days. in
which the United States 9th Air
Force alone dispatched more than
1000 big planes against key Nazi
targets despite uns atisfactory
weather conditions.


Drizzling rain in some sectors
failed to ground fighter bombers
based In France. Field dispatches
said they hammered away at enemy
communications and strong points
for the 18th straight day.

istry said.

rs lesser planes.


Skies over the Dover Strait were

craft fire echoed from the opposite
shore.


The Mediterranean Army Air

| The MAAF, summarizing the re-

staff had remained in part of the
chateau during the two years of

ments of the latter closely restrict
ed. The countess husband, a close

maps.


And that table over there was
where Pershing worked during Wis
its to the chateau, which quartered

war" she said.

1t was a solid. highly polished ta-

less tapestry.


"Dollmann,' she continued, "ar-
rived here February 7, 1912, and
lived here until they found him
dead in LIE Mans recently. He had
stayed in town overnight and after
his death the Germans announced

got around that he was made a goat

invasion"


Berlin radio on June 80 said

1t was speculated in London that
he might have been a bomb VIC
tim. Hitler later gave Dollmann a
posthumous decoration)


Shortly before the outbreak of
this war, the housekeeper continued,
British Field Marshal Lord Gort
and his staff came to the chateau
secretly to discuss defense plans
with the French. When hostilities
began, Lord Gort set up headquar-
tiers here with the Duke of Glou-
cester as his aide.


Rommel Came in March.


Rommel made his first apear-
ance at the chateau last March In
great secrecy, the housekeeper said.
After his first visit, Rommel came
often.


He would bring Doenitz, Sperre.
Won Runstedt and Others and
they'd always go to the second floor
for long conferences" she said.
They would leave in separate par
ties for inspection tours of coast
defenses."


For protection against air attack,
the Nazis had within sprinting dis
tance of the chateau a formidable
shelter. Made of concrete blocks
six feet square, it was equipped with
antl-eas doors, running hot and cold
water. beds, electric lights and air
conditioning.

IRUN, Spain, Aug. 2l.-Three
light Allied cruisers shelled al
most nonexiStent German de-
fenses in the Bayonne area of
Southwestern France before
dawn today.


Spanish residents of this border
town Is miles to the south had a
grandstand seat.

the coast south of Bordeaux evi-
IDENTIFY were feeling out German de-

reply from two or three coastal bat

South of Bayonne, Hitler's At
lantic Wall no longer exists. for the

lied column was reported to have
passed through Angouleme. 100 miles

plainly visible from the Spanish

tnodically for more than half an
hour. Splashes OF shells in the
war around the cruisers from the
light German counterfire were also
seen, but no hits were observed.

7:45 am and disappeared north
ward. but heavy explosions from the
Bayonne region continued as the
last remaining Germans apparently
went on with systematic destruc-
ton of their Notifications.

in battle with fleeing Nazis in the
area OF Sauzet, miles northeast
OF Montelimar. The latter town is
being mopped up. An American
column had reached the Rhone
north OF Montelimar in a surprise
thrust last week.


French forces sweeping westward
of the lower Rhone reached Uzes
and drove through Mines TODAY
One column thrust on southwest
toward the French-Spanish border
Other French units pushed out west
and northwest of Avignon, As miles
below Montelimar.


Toulon Base DESTROYED.


Air force headquarters declared
the great naval base of Toulon had
been destroyed by Allied bombing
and German demolitions before the
garrison surrendered.


Wreckage of scores of ships dots
the harbor, including two French
cruisers used as German barracks
and bombed by Allied planes. Sub
marine pens were wiped out, either
by demolitions or bombardment
and at least 10 submarines were
sunk at anchor"


The flying column under the COM
mand Of Brig. Gen. Frederick Butler
which reached the Montelimar area
Friday, after inflicting wholesale
punishment on at least one force of
$4,000 German troops. killing many
and possibly knocking out the re-
mainder, continued to spread out
through the entire region.


Yanks Drive Into Cagnes.


Reports from there said roads
were strewn with destroyed Ger
man transport and other vehicles.


American forces on the eastern
coastal flank late yesterday drove
into Cagnes, 10 miles northeast
of Cannes, and Vence, miles in
land due north of Cagnes-ad-
vances which placed them miles
from Nice and only 20 miles from
the Italian frontier.


Thousands of German troops fell
into Allied hands with the sur
render of the final holdout enemy
resistance in Marseille. The full
liberation Of Marseille and Toulon
gives the Allies adequate port facil-
tiles for any operations necessary,
not only for the military campaign.
but for rehabilitation of the lib
Grated areas.


Surrender OF forts on the St.
Mandrier Peninsula in the Toulon
area brought an end to fighting in
the coastal area.


The surrender was arranged
through 1t. Gen. Gotthold Schaefer
commanding the German oath Di-
vision and supreme Nan commander
in the Marseille region.


Coastal Batteries Bombarded.


The surrender of the St. Mandrier
garrison came after the enemy
coastal batteries were heavily bonn
barded by French, British and
American naval vessels-including
the French battleship Lorraine and
the British battleship Families.


Other elements of the fleet pene-
trated into the Gulf of Genoa, sink
ing one enemy vessel and possibly
sinking another.


Even while the last sporadic bursts
of fire were sweeping the streets OF
the ports of Southern France, Allied
supplied food, drugs and medicinal
supplies were being hurried into the
area and distributed among the
French natives.


The first shipments contained
flour. Meat and sugar followed.

captions OF the life that comes after death.

AS assistant kitchen director
and acting director for the past
three months of the District of
Columbia Chapter Red Cross
Canteen, Mrs. Paul c. Ollie does
a bangup job. You know how we
housewives struggle with plan
ming our own meals at home and
making them good and nourish-
ing with wartime rationing? Well,
how would you like to have to
plan luncheon for 400 people
every day, and have a good menu,
a varied menu and an inexpen-
sive one? That's what Mrs. Ollie
does and does we'll.


In summer, when the spacious
gardens behind the National Red
Cross headquarters can be used,
the Red Gross workers and serv-
ice men and women average be-
tween 500 and 600 for luncheon
each day, but in winter, when the
canteen goes inside, daily lunch
cons number around 400. There
is always one good hot dish
Hungarian goulash is great
favorite, Mrs. Ollie told us, and
then there are the delicious salads
and sandwiches prepared by the
volunteer workers themselves,
coffee, tea or milk and several
kinds of dessert from which to
choose. All the workers are VOL
unteer except the chief cook (who
does the main hot dish and the
soups and the dishwashers.


Menus are planned a week in
advance, Mrs. Ollie told us, and
although that may sound very
simple, often the foods that have
been so carefully planned ahead
aren't available at the market
when the time comes to order
them. Then something has to be
substituted and that's where Mrs.
Dille's ingenuity comes in-she
never seems to be stumped.


Mrs. Ollie has to cope with
ration points, too, just like the
rest Of us. The points are al
lotted by the ration board every
two months-the amount based
on the number of people served
in the preceding two months.
You can imagine how much
figuring out just how far those
points will go takes. Then, too,
all the food deliveries coming in
have to be carefully checked
after the menus have been made
out and the orders given. It's a
full-time job all right, and Mrs.
Ollie Is there every morning from
8 o'clock until 4 or S in the after
noon five days a week. Saturday
mornings she goes to the Blood
Donor Center and helps at the
canteen there (you know, OF
course, that the donors are
always given some sort of hot
drink or refreshment after they
have given blood.


For the past winter Mrs. Ollie
has been going out with the
night mobile canteen every Fri
day night and during the Red
Cross War Fund Drive she takes
time out from the D. C. Canteen
to 90 over to the Chamber of
Commerce Building every Tues
day and help serve luncheon to
the workers who report collec-
tions. Add to this that she takes
care Of her own cozy apartment
and cooks delicious meals for
herself and husband and you
have a pretty full schedule-and
a very worthwhile one.

British troop landings on the
Greek mainland and their rapid
advance against slight German op-
position have opened another long
shattered window OF Hitler's For
tress Europe" permitting a clear
view into what lies behind. First
hand reports by American news
paper correspondents accompanying
the British expeditionary forces give
us accurate and colorful accounts of
conditions and prospects. The lib
Grated area is thus far confined to
the Peloponnesus, the rugged pen
insula which forms the southern
extension of Greece into the Medi-
terranean. Traditionally poor and
backward, the Peloponnesus per-
haps does not typify conditions
throughout Greece. Nevertheless,
this sample is probably not far
below the average.


The descriptions thus far penned
by our correspondents give tragic
picture and forecast serious prob
lens for the near future. The gen.
eral population, while not literally
starving, is devitalized by prolonged
hunger and uncared-for diseases,
especially malaria. However, this low
state of vitality has not inhibited
political passions, which are running
high. 1t should be remembered that
the modern Greeks, like their fore
bears Of antiquity, take their politics
violently and are prone to factional
strife. Prewar -quarrels have been
both complicated and intensified by
the years of Axis occupation. When
the Germans overran Greece, the
boldest spirits took to the inacces-
sible mountains and there formed
guerrilla bands under local leaders
OF varied character. This patriotic
movement was never unified, but
evolved into factions which came to
hate each other almost as much as
they did the Germans. The upshotS
was sporadic civil war going on
parallel to the war against the in
vaders, and Of course the general
population suffered from both. This
led certain elements to cooperate
partially with the Germans by form
ing security battalions" to maintain
order and prevent depredations by
rival patriot guerrillas, some of
which were little better than brig
and bands. This security" element
should be distinguished from the
much smaller group of outright COL
laborationists who went over entirely
to the German side and proflteered
therefrom.


However, the guerrillas apparently
consider all not actively with them
as quislings and want literally to
exterminate them and confiscate
their property. The British authori-
ties are having hard time prevent
Ing wholesale killings and lootings
which might be the prelude to a
ferocious civil war and general
chaos. This ominous situation in the
Peloponnesus will very likely be
duplicated in other parts of Greece;
and, for that matter, may be ex-
pected elsewhere In the Balkans as
they are liberated from German
domination. The outlook is thus a
dubious and troubled one.

silence. The stiffness of the night
was ominous when we reached shore


No broadsides of bullets, no bursts

We slogged down the open ramp

main assault force. Everything

beaches-tanks, jeeps, trucks and ar.

When the beachhead was won

beaches through marshes until they
reached the regular roads, including

Berlin reports heavy Red attacks on
the Isthmus of Perekop, the narrow
neck connecting the Crimea with
the mainland, together with simul-
taneous operations across the sand
spits and lagoons farther to the
eastward. Following customary pro-

nounced this offensive, waiting until
it gets well under way. But the Ger
man high command often speaks
first on such occasions, and its re-

little doubt it conforms to the basic
facts.


Ever since the great Red often

man land link with the Crimea, it

it's mixed German and Romanian
garrison being dependent upon COM
munications by sea. This was re-
latively easy so long as the nearby
port Of Odessa remained in Axis
hands. But the capture of that
metropolis intensifies the Crimea's
isolation. Indeed, this is the logical
moment for the Soviet high COM
mand to eliminate the Crimean
bastion as we'll

possessor. This diamond-shaped
peninsula, about the size of Mary
land, dominates the Black Sea and
likewise cuts off the smaller Sea of
Azov, which empties into the Black
Sea through the narrow Kerch
Strait separating the Crimea from
the Caucasus. The Germans were
driven from their Caucasian bridge
head late last autumn, so it is likely

Christmas. the extra special

STROBE into the room.

eyes widening in awe.

decorated Christmas tree and
brought the room to life.


There's my puppy" Nubbins
cried. and went to the tree
which was loaded with more

nation by kid loving Americans


who also mailed his parents


more than $500 to give the boy


real Christmas.

tors have warned that the black
puppy may be without a master

around.

By the Associated Press.


LONDON, June 26.-RAF Mos
quitos flying from Britain main
tanned steady Allied air pressure
on the enemy both in Normady
and the German homeland last
night, while medium and heavy
bombers from Italy hit Buda-
pest, Hungary's capital.


Continuing the Allied air opera
tions which yesterday kept five air
armadas-four from Britain and one
from Italy-drumming German in
stallations in France virtually all
day, the Mosquitoes attacked Ger
man troop concentrations, railroads
and supply dumps near the French
battlefront and industrial objectives
in the German city of Homberg
northwest of Duisberg.


Unfavorable weather this morn
ing threatened to limit today's op-
erations over the beachhead sectors.


fThe German radio said violent


air battles ragged this morning


over the area around Vienna and


further east along the Danube


Valley as German fighters


attacked formations of Allied


bombers - presumably striking


from Italy. The broadcast was


recorded in New York by the


Federal Communications Com


mission.)


Supply Dumps Set Afire.


Beyond the Normandy front
lines the Mosquitoes last night left
German supply dumps hidden in the
forest of Bretonne on the Seine a
mass of flames. Crewmen said the
fires stretched miles and were ad-
vancing in series of semicircles
when they left.


The Mosquitoes bombed German
troops in the village of Evrecy,
southwest of Caen. Railroads north
of Laigle and at Argentan were
among other targets.


Supreme headquarters announced
that although most of yesterdays
tactical assaults were directed
against enemy fuel dumps and rail-
roads, some American Thunderbolt
dive-bombers struck German gun
emplacements in Cherbourg.


About $500 warplanes participated
In yesterdays attacks, ranging from
Pas-de Calais to the Southern coast
of France.


Two of the mighty fleets, one
American and one British, battered
the Nazi winged bomb emplace-
ments at Pas-de- Calais. Absent
from English skies during daylight
yesterday, the robots began coming
over again during the night, but
many were blasted before they got
across the Channel.


Heavy Bombers Strike Repeatedly.
American Flying Fortresses and
Liberators struck three times from
Britain during the day. Another
force of the United States four
engined bombers struck into France
from Italy.


Medium, light and fighter bomb
ers and fighters swarmed over and
beyond the Normandy battle areas
throughout the day in steady sup
port of ground forces.


Allied losses for the day were
placed at 43 planes, including 20
heavy bombers. Fifty-nine Germans
were downed.

PACIFIC FLEET HEADQUAR-
TIERS, Pearl Harbor, Sept. 3d.
Taking three more strides along
the stepping stones that lead
westward to the Philippines,
American forces today controlled
nine islands of the strategic
Palau group and a new airfield.


Admiral Chester w. Nimitz an
nounced last night that Kongauru
Ngesbus, with its 4,8OO-foot fighter
strip, and an unnamed island "have
been made secure"


American forces thus increased
the usefulness of the excellent cap
tured airdrome on Peleliu, which the
Japanese expended almost 5000 men
to defend. This field and others in
the Palaus are little more than 500
miles east of the Philippines.


Flying Facilities Aided.


BY invading the three islets the
Americans drove Japanese artillery
out of range of the Peleliu bomber
field.


Added to the flying facilities of
the Palaus, the Americans have
other bases close to the Philippines
and Gen. MacArthur's communique
today indicated he is making good
use Of them. He said planes, flying
from them, sank or damaged II
Japanese craft, ranging from small
freighters to barges.


Six craft were sunk or damaged
of Mindanao, in the Southern Phil
ippines and seven off the Celebes
Others were bagged off Borneo
Boeroe and Halmahera.


Bitter fighting by the japanese to
defend their Palaus strongholds un-
derscored the Importance they at
tach to the American thrust toward
the Philippines.


9,772 Japs Killed.


American marines and soldiers
have killed 8,717 Japanese on Pele-
liu and 1,055 on nearby Angaur, a
total of 9,772. Fighting has ragged
since September Is and the Japa-
nese are battling to the bitter end
from isolated pockets on Peleliu.
The three nearby islets were in
vaded Wednesday and Admiral
Nimitz said Ngesebus was captured
the same day. The next day Kon-
gauru was secured along with the
nearby unnamed island.
The landings were made under the
cover of warships and carrier planes

and German troops were locked

reau in broadcast recorded by the

evacuating their trapped forces,
adding greatly to Axis casualties.


The information bureau reported
that 10000 Germans and Roman
ians were killed in the final three
day assault which toppled Sevasto-
pol last Tuesday, and that more
than $4,000 were killed in the over
all campaign which began April 8.

planes. The communique declared

in men"

claimed, however, that Nazi troops

persing seven Russian rifle divisions
and parts of one artillery and anti
aircraft division.

front there were no essential

apartments and casualties in

1t was the heaviest raid on the

The best unofficial estimates were

not all of them penetrated the ter

was the most widespread of any at
tack of the last year and casualties
were left in half a dozen districts.

Twelve persons were known to

struck preserve factory and homes

NEW DELHI; April 15.-An
Allied force apparently was
moving eastward from Dimapur
today in an effort to clear the
Maya Hills road to Kohima and
the Manipur Valley of Japanese
road blocks.


The road is one of the two jungle
communication routes to the threat
ened Imphal Valley of Eastern
India.


Todays communique from the
Southeast Asia command said small
japanese parties were still holding
fast on the Rishenpur- Silchar trail,
the other route southwest of Imphal,
although the enemy was meeting
with heavy casualties in his at
tempts to choke off this important
supply base.


Although progress was reported
in clearing the enemy from the
road running northwest of Kohima.
so miles north of Imphal, the COM
munique said mo important change
had taken place around Kohima
itself or in the sectors south and
east of Imphal.


Front line dispatches yesterday
said the Japanese had reached the
Bishenpur- Silchar trail leading into
the Bengal f1atlands and Allied COM
munication lines.


Trail $50 Miles Long.
The jungle trail leading from
Bishenpur. II miles southwest of
Imphal, to Silchar, the terminal of
a spur line connecting with the
Bengal-Assam Railway, is 10 miles
airline long, but about $50 miles for
coolie and mulepack parties making
the tortuous hike. Silchar is I'm
phal's nearest railhead.
Dispatches indicated the Jap
anese infiltration was small, and
said a dozen casualties had been in
f1icted on the enemy in the first
brush along the trail.


japanese snipers were still active
along Imphals other outlet, the road
through Kohima to Dimapur on the
Bengal-Assam railway, but the
Allied communique said offensive
operations against enemy road
blocks on the Kohima -Dimapur
stretch of the road were making
progress.


In this connection, a front-line
account confirmed previous reports
that small Japanese parties at one
time did penetrate the outskirts of
the defended area of Kohima, but
said the enemy party was liquidated.
Forty-nine Japanese dead were
counted and some prisoners taken
The rest withdrew into the hills to
the northeast.


Talked With Deserter.
In his surprise visit to Imphal last
Saturday, it was disclosed, Admiral
Lord Louis Mountbatten, Southeast
Asia commander, had a five minute
talk with Japanese deserter, a "a
year-old gunner, who left his unit
to go native and ran into a British
patrol.


I've seen japanese prisoners be-
fore but never one who was a
deserter," Mountbatten said.


The communique said 1t. Gen
Joseph w. Stilwell's offensive in
Northern Burma was continuing to
make progress southwark toward
Myitkyina and the Mandalay rail-
way, and indicated patrols had
penetrated close to Kamaing, the
next important objective. Kamaing
is about 20 miles south of the last
announced Allied position.


Allied aircraft were exceedingly
active over all fronts, bombing and
strafing, the communique said.

The Sturdiness Of American cruiser
construction was underlined today
when the Navy revealed that two of
the ships critically damaged by the
Japs in battle off the Solomon
Islands in November, 1912, now are
ready to return to action.


One Of them, the Minneapolis
gave the Japs such deadly hail of
fire that the Toxic radio, in an
nouncing her sinking" claimed a
battleship. The other, the New Or
leans, had her bow and forward gun
turret shot off completely but man
aged to limp into Tulagi Harbor
for emergency repairs. Both ships
reached Pacific Coast repair yards
and were refitted for service in rec
ord time.


Marked End Of Jap Effort.


What the Japs ignored in their
radio broadcasts, the Navy pointed
out in announcing that the two
cruisers again are with the fleet,
was that the engagement put big
black period after Jap efforts to re-
inforce their troops on Guadalcanal.
Nor did they play up the fact that
the dwindling Jap navy lost two
large destroyers-maybe cruisers
four smaller destroyers, two trans
ports and one cargo ship during the
engagement.


Literally cut apart by torpedoes
aft of the forward gun turret, the
New Orleans was out Of action early,
but not before she had done her
share in sending five enemy ships to
the bottom. Then with only bulk
heads holding out the seas, she wal
lowed into Tulagi harbor. There
her crew used logs to reinforce the
bulkheads for a 1,700-mile run to
Australia, where a temporary bow
was fitted for the long trip back to
the United States.


Meantime, at Puget Sound Navy
Yard, workers prefabricated a new
bow while the cruiser limped home.
1t was ready when she arrived.
Machinery was borrowed from other
cruisers-a new turret was taken
from a ship under overhaul-to
speed her back to sea in record
time.


Aided Sinking Of Three Ships.


Torpedoes and shells from enemy
warships struck the Minneapolis in
the midst of the same flaming bat
tie. Fire engulfed her from the
waterline to superstructure. But
she already had done her part,
definitely sinking one ship and
helping destroy at least two more.


Despite her damage, Capt. Charles
E. Rosendahl of Cleburne, Tex
now a rear admiral-brought the
Minneapolis into Tulagi. There Sea-
bees joined with her crew in making
her seaworthy for a long trip to
the Mare Island Navy Yard, where
repairs were completed.


Three other American cruisers
participated in the battle-one, the
Northampton, was lost; another, the
Pensacola, was damaged and has
been repaired; the fifth has not
been named.


Opposing that force were at least
eight Japanese destroyers, and the
Navy said, possibly several cruisers"
guarding troop transports and sup
ply ships. ....

ROME, Aug. 19.-Maj. Gen
Alexander M. Patch's 7th Army,
extending its Southern France
beachhead to 1000 square miles,
has speared westward to within
81 miles of Marseille in a drive
flanking Toulon and has plunged
at least 80 miles inland, Allied
headquarters announced today


A front 20 miles broad has beer
driven to the north and behind
Toulon, the French naval base al
which American bombers yesterday
blasted the half submerged French
battleship Strassbourg in an effort
to silence her big guns which were
opposing the Allied attack.


Latest announcements put Ameri-
can and French forces only 6 miles
northeast of Toulon, but other ad-
vance units, speeding over a net
work of inland roads, were pointed
directly toward the Rhone Valley
through routes which bypass Tou-

Other towns taken were Sollies-

In the approach to the naval

Washington Lions, fighting to get
back in the pennant race in the
Eastern Hockey League, tonight en-
tertain on Uline ice the Dead End
Kids" of the loop-the Baltimore
Blades, sextet that has whipped
the locals three times in three starts.


The Lions, in third place and
three points behind the second place
Blades, have rested since last Fri
day night, when they defeated the
Philadelphia Falcons, 5 to 8, and
Coach Charley Good feels that the
Washingtonians have a good chance
to upset the Baltimore jinx tonight.


The Lions defensive system has
been considerably strengthened by
the return of Jimmy Wilson, clever
young defenseman, who has been on
the sidelines with an injured leg.
Wilson, teamed with 17-year-old
Tony Dorm, rugged dependable,
may be able to give some support to
young Emile Francis, diminutive
Lion goalie, who so far this season
has borne the brunt of the attack.
The Washington offense will be
built around Alan Percival, the ver-
satile forward, who is tied for fourth
place among Eastern League scorers
with Ray Pavell of the Blades. Each
has scored 25 points.

text:
The German high command-.whether
Hitler, his generals or both-made one
supreme gamble to gain time a few
weeks ago-a gamble which lost-and
the day of final defeat as a result has
been brought appreciably nearer.


Throwing an immense number of
tanks, many of which were drawn from
France, Italy, Poland, the Netherlands
and other areas, into drive for Kiev,
the Germans some weeks ago sought
break-through which might force gen.
eral Russian retreat. The cost was
heavy, and thousands of tanks were
reported destroyed as the Reds gave
ground slowly for time


Suddenly the tide turned, and the
Russians hit back strongly after mis-
leading the Nazis to some extent by the
opening of an offensive on the Baltic
front. Overwhelmed after defending
their gains for several days. the Nazis
weakened and began to yield, until on
Thursday came the announcement that
everywhere along a 185-mile front the
Germans were falling back in a rout in
which the high command had lost con-
troll over the troops and in which local
commands we're out of contact with
garrisons which were being surrounded
and captured or killed.


The high-water mark of the German
advance put two cities-Korosten and
zhitomir-in Nazi hands, and at these
points resistance against the Russian
counterattack was most persistent.


The Reds were hitting powerfully in
two offensives simultaneously, one
aimed at Vitebsk, important railroad
center blocking the path to the Baltic
states, and the other stemming out from
klev toward Korosten and Zhitomir.
Monday the Moscow bulletins reported
that the Ukrainian Army had regained
Is miles and that the Baltic thrust had
moved forward miles, the Nazis losing
$4,000 men in dead during the day.


Tuesday it was reported that impor-
tant railroad centers at Andrushevka
and Berdichev had been captured and
on Wednesday the Reds were fighting
in the outskirts of Korosten and zhito-
mir. Sixteen German counterattacks in
the Vitebsk area on the Baltic front
were beaten back and the Reds moved
slowly forward.


Thursday and Friday came the well
come news that the rout of the Germans
was underway, that more than 5000
populated places have beeen captured
and that the Reds are now only 43
miles from the pre-1939 Polish border
and only 80 miles from the Dniester
River border of Rumania. The Reds
we're far beyond Zhitomir, which was
reported late Friday to have been cap
tured. Gen. Won Mannstein finds him.
self in a critical situation in which he
must fight for his life against the en-
velopment which is impending. Obser-
vers are describing his Inflated drive
toward Kiev as one of the worst Nazi
plumbers of the war.

Disclosure that Prien is prisoner
lifts partly for the first time in
three and one-half years the total
mystery covering the fate of this
most famous of Germany'S U-boat
commanders.


1t was on October a. 1899, when
the war was less than six weeks old,
that Prien, lieutenant commander,
startled the world by slipping into
the closely guarded British naval
base at Scapa Flow and sinking the
29O00-ton British battleship Royal
Oak with torpedo. Eight hundred
and ten of the Royal Oaks officers
and men were killed.


Decorated by Hitler.


Prien then managed to get his
submarine safely out of the British
stronghold and returned to Germany
where Adolf Hitler personally deco
rated him with the Knights Cross
of the Iron Cross and promoted him
to the rank of commander.


For this ceremony, a special joint
meeting of the German and foreign
press-an unusual occurrence-wasI
called in Berlin, and Prien, then 80,
made a short, snappy but modest
speech. He didn't seem to relish his
role as hero.


His crew, group of young and
aggressive lads who stood behind |
him as he talked, seemed to enjoy
the sudden limelight.


Prien and his crew were taken to
several schools to INSPIRE" youth.


Editorials hailed him as a typical
product of Hitlerean superman
teachings.


Later when news came that
Prien's submarine was lost and the
commander and crew missing, deep
gloom spread over the youth of Ger
many. Propaganda Minister Joseph
Goebbels seized on the occasion to
again dramatic Prien as the ideal
German.


Was Nazi Hero of Heroes.


The propaganda ministry empha-
sized that Prien had preferred
danger and sacrifice to the safety
and comfort of an easy assign
ment.


Prien claimed to have torpedoed
and damaged the British battle
cruiser Repulse at the same time
he sank the Royal Oak, but this the
British denied.


How he got in and out of Scapa
Flow has never been satisfactorily
explained, although many legends
quickly grew up about the exploit.
Subsequently, during several
cruises in 1910, Prien was credited
by the Germans with sinking more
than $4,000 tons of British shipping.
He was the German underseas serv-
ices hero of heroes.


Then came a curiously anti
climatic denouement. On May 2,
1941, the British radio reported that
he had been missing since April 13,
l941. How the British knew this
never was disclosed.


Reluctantly the German high
command on May %, 1941, acknowl-
edged that Prien and his submarine
had failed to return from cruise.
Presumably he was dead. His name
never was mentioned publicly again.


Now it is disclosed that Prien,
the toast of the German Navy, suf-
fered a fate that many submariners
consider worse than death-he was
captured. How and when remain
secret

Two young Germans were sup
